Recommendation 38 Vitamin E (800 IU α-tocopherol daily) should be prescribed to non-diabetic adults with histologically confirmed NASH aiming for improvement of liver enzymes and histology. (BM) Grade of recommendation B – Strong consensus (100 % agreement) Commentary The efficacy of Vitamin E as an anti-oxidant to ameliorate biochemical and/or histological abnormalities of NASH has been investigated in a number of trials ( , – ). There is, however, a great heterogeneity among these trials regarding study power, entry criteria, dosage of vitamin E, formulations of vitamin E used, additional use of other anti-oxidants or other drugs and histologic data to assess outcomes. Despite these limitations, the following conclusions can be drawn regarding adults with NASH ( , ): 1. the use of vitamin E is associated with an improvement of liver enzymes (decrease in ALT, AST), 2. trials evaluating NASH features in paired liver biopsies show improvement in steatosis, inflammation, and ballooning and resolution of steatohepatitis in patients treated with vitamin E when compared to controls, and 3. vitamin E has limited or no effect on hepatic fibrosis. In the largest RCT (PIVENS trial) the predefined primary endpoint was achieved in a significantly greater number of participants receiving oral vitamin E (800 IU·d −1 for two years) compared to placebo (42% vs. 19%, p<0.001, number needed to treat =4.4)( ). Re-analysis of the PIVENS trial showed that ALT responses were more frequent in the vitamin E recipients and were associated with the NAFLD Activity Score (NAS), but not fibrosis scores ( ). Interestingly, vitamin E had an added effect on the improvement of ALT, NAS, and fibrosis scores obtained by weight loss > 2.0 kg ( ). The authors of a meta-analysis of 19 trials (135 967 participants) studying a variety of populations in whom the presence or absence of NASH was not specifically addressed came to the conclusion that vitamin E dosage > 400 IU·d −1 was associated with an increased risk for all-cause mortality and should be avoided ( ). The authors found no significant treatment effect of antioxidants on all-cause mortality or liver-related mortality. In another meta-analysis no beneficial effect of anti-oxidant treatment on liver biochemistry and histology was reported ( ). Recommendation 39 Until further data regarding their efficacy are available, antioxidants (e.g. vitamin C, resveratrol, anthocyanin, bayberries) cannot be recommended to treat NAFL / NASH. (BM) Grade of recommendation 0 – Strong consensus (100 % agreement) Commentary In twelve overweight/obese men with NAFLD, oral resveratrol (3000 mg) for eight weeks had no effect on insulin resistance, steatosis, abdominal fat distribution and plasma lipids or antioxidant activity. ALT and AST levels, however, increased significantly in the resveratrol group ( ). In a randomized controlled trial, 2 × 150 mg resveratrol p. o. for three months was found to improve AST, ALT, LDL and total cholesterol, HOMA-IR and inflammation mediators in 30 normal weight men with NAFLD on ultrasound ( ). One 500 mg capsule of resveratrol together with lifestyle intervention was more effective than lifestyle intervention alone in overweight patients regarding improvement in ALT, inflammatory cytokines and hepatic steatosis; this randomized controlled trial obviously was published in duplicate ( , ). Bayberry juice containing high levels of polyphenols had no effect on anthropometric measures and HOMA-IR in Chines normal weight patients with NAFLD on ultrasound ( ). In a randomized controlled pilot trial, the flavonoid anthocyanin (320 mg p. o. for twelve weeks) decreased ALT and the 2-hour loading glucose level ( ). Oral coenzymeQ10 supplementation was reported to reduce waist circumference, serum AST levels and blood total anti-oxidant capacity ( ). In NAFLD patients, a vitamin C intake below the recommended daily allowance has been reported in epidemiological studies, suggesting an association between dietary habits, disease and vitamin C deficiency. The presently available RCTs have not found an effect of vitamin C superior to that of placebo. Thus, the role of vitamin C in NAFLD should be investigated in future adequately controlled RCTs ( ). Abnormally low choline levels have been implicated in the pathogenesis of PN associated liver disease of which some morphological features resemble NAFLD/NASH ( ). A secondary analysis of food questionnaires from 664 participants of three NASH Clinical Research Network trials showed that in postmenopausal women a decreased choline intake was associated with increased fibrosis ( ). Along this line, data from the Shanghai Women’s and Men’s Health Study suggest that higher dietary choline intake may be associated with a lower risk of NAFLD ( ). On the other hand, a close relation between plasma free choline levels and the grade of liver steatosis and fibrosis has been observed in NASH ( ). There is no data from choline intervention trials. Compared to placebo, oral supplementation of L-carnitine (1 g b.i.d. for 24 weeks) was effective in reducing TNF-α and CRP and in improving liver function, glucose plasma level, lipid profile, HOMA-IR, and histological manifestations of NASH ( ). In diabetic NAFLD patients, oral carnitine-orotate (3 × 824 mg for twelve weeks) was associated with significant improvement in ALT, hepatic steatosis and HbA1c in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial ( ). These are preliminary results and, therefore L-carnitine cannot be recommended yet. 4.9 For patients with NAFL / NASH, can supplementation with omega-3 fatty acids when compared to no such supplementation be recommended to a. reduce the risk for comorbidity (e.g. cardiovascular, diabetes), b. improve liver enzymes, c. improve NASH histology, d. slow progression to cirrhosis, e. reduce incidence of HCC, f. reduce mortality? Recommendation 41 Nutritional supplements containing selected probiotics or synbiotics can be used to improve liver enzymes in NAFL / NASH patients. (BM) Grade of recommendation 0 – Consensus (89 % agreement) Commentary A systematic review identified nine full text papers of randomized clinical trials evaluating probiotics, prebiotics or synbiotics in the treatment of adult NAFLD of which six were excluded due to methodological deficits ( ). Grade of recommendation GPP – Majority agreement (71 % agreement) Commentary An increasing number (30–35 %) of adult ICU patients are obese and at least 5 % are morbidly obese ( ). Nutrition support of such patients is challenging and one of the most difficult aspects in clinical nutrition. Obesity has an impact on the incidence and severity of comorbidities and patient outcome. According to ASPEN guidelines such patients should be cared for according to the basic principles of critical care nutrition aiming for a high protein intake (2.0–2.5 g▪kg −1 IBW▪d −1 ) for the preservation of lean body mass but a hypocaloric regimen (25 kcal▪kg −1 IBW▪d −1 ) aiming for the reduction of fat mass and insulin resistance ( ). Recommendation 45 In otherwise eligible obese NAFL / NASH patients without cirrhosis, after weight reduction diets and intensive lifestyle interventions have failed, bariatric surgery should be proposed. (BM) Grade of recommendation B – Strong consensus (100 % agreement) Commentary Lifestyle intervention, although effective in some patients, is not sufficient to achieve long-term weight loss and resolution of NASH. It is estimated that only 10% of patients who commit to a lifestyle intervention lose more than 10% of their weight, even when the intervention involves a multidisciplinary approach ( ). Currently, no drug treatment has been shown effective, but many compounds are under investigation. Bariatric surgery is a potential treatment option in NAFLD, in particularly its progressive form NASH. Indeed, the majority of obese patients undergoing bariatric surgery are obese and have associated NAFLD ( ). There are no systematic randomized controlled trials that evaluated any bariatric surgical procedure to specifically treat NAFLD or NASH. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies reporting on 766 paired liver biopsies showed that the pooled proportion of patients with improvement or resolution in steatosis was 92%, in steatohepatitis was 81%, in fibrosis was 66% and for complete resolution of NASH was 70% ( ). These findings are corroborated by the Lille data from France ( ). Using a state-transition model, Klebanoff et al ( ) aimed to assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of surgery or intensive lifestyle intervention to manage NASH. In overweight patients, surgery increased QALYs for all patients regardless of fibrosis stage, but it was cost-effective only for patients with F3 fibrosis. In one series, cirrhosis was diagnosed intraoperatively in 4% and fibrosis in 37% of patients undergoing bariatric surgery ( ). Perioperative mortality of bariatric surgery is lower in patients without cirrhosis compared to patients with compensated or decompensated cirrhosis (0.3% vs 0.9% and 16.3%) ( ). (BM) Grade of recommendation GPP – Strong consensus (100% agreement) Commentary to recommendations 50 and 51 In general, energy requirements in compensated LC patients are not higher than in healthy individuals (see statement 4 and recommendation 2). Moreover, LC patients have a decreased physical activity level ( , ) and thus a decreased energy expenditure due to physical activity. Cirrhotic patients during the natural course of the disease tend to spontaneously decrease their dietary intake ( , ). This is of special relevance in the subgroup (up to 35 % of LC patients) of hyper-metabolic LC patients ( , , ) or in those with advanced cirrhosis with complications when energy expenditure may be increased. Therefore, measurement of energy expenditure is recommended whenever possible (see recommendation 1). Oral, enteral or parenteral nutrition have been utilized in short and long term studies in decompensated and/or malnourished cirrhotic patients with some advantages either in morbidity or in mortality ( ). The proportion of overweight or obese LC patients has increased even in cohorts on the wait list for transplantation ( , , ). In chronic liver disease, obesity has been identified as an independent risk factor for a worse clinical outcome ( , ). Obesity has been proposed to promote portal hypertension. Portal hypertension could be ameliorated by lifestyle intervention for 16 weeks using hypocaloric diet and increased exercise in LC patients ( ). Therefore, an increased energy intake is not recommended in obese cirrhotic patients. 5.4 In all cirrhotic patients, is increased as compared to normal protein assumption/intake always needed to face increased protein turnover and catabolism? Increased protein intake is generally well tolerated and safe in cirrhotic patients and ameliorates protein anabolism as shown in previous studies. ( , ). In intervention studies implementing high protein intakes improvement in arm muscle circumference, handgrip strength and albumin was observed ( , – ). (BM) Grade of recommendation GPP – Strong consensus (100% agreement) Commentary Patients with cirrhosis may present deficiencies in water-soluble vitamins, particularly thiamine, and lipid soluble vitamins such as vitamin D ( , ). There are no reports which systematically evaluate the requirement of micronutrients in LC. Like in other conditions, the administration of micronutrients has no proven therapeutic effect apart from the prevention or correction of deficiency states. Zinc and vitamin A supplements by improving dysgeusia may indirectly improve food intake and nutritional state ( , ). Zinc and selenium deficiency have been observed in patients with alcoholic as well as non-alcoholic liver disease ( – ). An impressive association between HE and zinc deficiency has been described in case reports ( , ). Randomized controlled trials, however, showed no therapeutic effect of oral zinc supplementation on HE ( – ). Oral zinc supplementation can increase urea production capacity when previously subnormal plasma levels are normalized ( ). In a pragmatic approach, liberal supplementation is recommended in the first two weeks of nutritional support, because the laboratory diagnosis of a specific trace element or vitamin deficiency may be costlier and would delay commencing supplementation. After successful treatment of portal hypertension by transjugular intrahepatic stent-shunt (TIPS), LC patients on normal food (according to ESPEN recommendations) were able to improve their body composition ( , ). In a well conducted prospective trial measuring total body nitrogen the nocturnal administration of ONS has been shown to be more effective in improving total body protein status than daytime ONS ( ). Previously, a late evening carbohydrate snack has been shown to improve protein metabolism in LC ( , , ). In their systematic review Tsien and coworkers ( ) showed that a late evening snack improved nitrogen balance, irrespective of the composition or type of formulation used. They conclude that shortening periods without food by late evening snack is a promising concept to reverse anabolic resistance and sarcopenia of cirrhosis. In the very rare case of a “protein intolerant” LC patient developing encephalopathy when ingesting normal amounts of mixed protein, a vegetable protein diet may be beneficial. A number of reviews have addressed this issue ( – ) but there is no data from randomized controlled trials comparing isocaloric and isonitrogenous regimens. One study ( ) was uncontrolled and in a more recent study nutritional therapy using a vegetable protein diet was compared to no therapy ( ). There are no data available from trials comparing a standard enteral formula and an enteral formula enriched in BCAA in LC patients. BCAA-enriched formulas, however, have been used in trials demonstrating improved survival in severely malnourished ASH and LC patients ( , , , ) or mental state in a highly selected group of protein intolerant LC patients with encephalopathy ( ). In the two largest trials (174 and 646 patients) oral BCAA supplementation (12 and 24 months) was useful to prevent progressive hepatic failure and to improve surrogate markers and health related quality of life ( , ). In LC patients after an episode of HE, BCAA supplementation for twelve months improved minimal HE and muscle mass but the recurrence of overt HE was not decreased vs the control group ( ). In a retrospective analysis, BCAA supplementation was associated with better survival in sarcopenic but not in non-sarcopenic LC patients ( ). In trials reporting beneficial effects on mental state and/or protein metabolism BCAA were given at doses of 0.20–0.25 g·kgBW-1·d −1 ( , , , ) or 30 g·d −1 ( , ). In a Cochrane meta-analysis, overall a beneficial effect of BCAA on mental state was found ( ) but there are unresolved issues regarding trial methodology ( , ). Based on the pathophysiology of ascites a moderate dietary sodium intake (60 mmol/day) is usually recommended. Therefore, great care should be taken to ensure adequate nutrition when prescribing a sodium restricted diet. Such intestinal failure associated liver disease (IFALD) and PNALD are difficult to separate in the individual patient and occur in up to 60 % of infants and up to 85 % of neonates who require long-term PN for intestinal failure ( , ). This is reflected in the term PNAC that is frequently used in the pediatric literature for this condition ( ), whereas the term PNALD has been used in both adult and pediatric patients ( , , ). In infants and neonates, mortality is high, up to 40 %, and PNAC has become a major indication for pediatric LT ( ). Strong consensus (100% agreement) Commentary Cholestatic liver injury occurs in 50 % of patients on long-term home PN ( ). In 1985, Bowyer and colleagues ( ) described steatohepatitis in nine out of 60 patients on long-term PN. Liver injury persisted for a median of 15 months (8 to 95) and progressed to cirrhosis in three patients. In their seminal paper Stanko and colleagues ( ) studied adults who had been on PN for one year. They found normal liver enzymes in those who had no or only modest loss of intestine while 4/6 patients with massive loss of intestine developed progressive cholestasis and steatohepatitis four to ten months after the initiation of PN. Their observation demonstrated that liver injury can occur not only as a sequel of PN – termed PNALD – but also by intestinal failure – termed IFALD. In clinical practice a clear distinction between IFALD or PNALD more often than not is difficult ( ). Grau and colleagues analyzed the association of liver disease and PN in 756 ICU patients on PN and/or EN ( ). They showed that the patients who developed liver injury had a characteristic profile in the way that they had a higher multiple organ dysfunction score on admission, they were septic, and they were treated with total PN. In adults, IFALD/PNALD is related to female gender, age, length of time on PN, total caloric intake, and lipid or glucose overload ( , ). The pathogenesis of IFALD/PNALD is thought to be multifactorial including factors like disturbance of enterohepatic bile acid cycling, systemic infection, bacterial overgrowth, absence of enteral nutrients and composition of PN ( , , ). Both lack and excess of specific components of PN are being discussed as causal for PNALD. The fatty acid composition of lipid emulsions ( ) as well as choline deficiency ( ), and manganese toxicity ( , ) have been linked to the occurrence of hepatic steatosis and cholestasis in adults and children. 7.4 In adults / children, can specialized nutrition protocols when compared to no such protocols improve/prevent a. biochemical signs of hepatocyte lesion, b. impaired liver function, c. abnormal liver histology, d. chronic liver disease? Recommendation 83 In infants, children and adults, specialized nutrition protocols making optimal use of EN should be implemented. (BM) Grade of recommendation B – Strong consensus (92% agreement) Commentary In infants and neonates, a number of reports suggest that the institution of specialized nutrition protocols is beneficial in achieving intestinal rehabilitation. Such protocols aim at limiting the infusion of soy-bean based lipid ( – ) and maximizing oral and enteral stimulation ( – ) and administering cyclic PN ( , , ). A retrospective study showed that the implementation of feeding guidelines resulted in decreased times without nutrition, shorter duration of PN support, and significantly fewer infants developed PNALD after guideline implementation ( ). In a multiple-variable analysis septic episodes (odds ratio 3.23), days of lipid >2.5 g·kg −1 ·d −1 (odds ratio 1.04), and 60 days of maximal lipid (odds ratio 10) were found to be the key elements for the development of PNAC ( ). A pilot study comparing standard (3.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 ) vs reduced (1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 ) lipid dose showed a slower rise of cholestasis markers using reduced lipid doses ( ). The role of a limited lipid administration ( ) is also strengthened by reports of a beneficial effect of a fish-oil emulsion given at 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 when compared to traditional soy bean emulsions infused at 1–4 g·kg −1 ·d −1 ( – ). As a note of caution, the extent to which there is an overlap of cases reported in six separate publications of one group is unclear ( – , ). In a recent ESPGHAN position paper ( ) early EN limiting i. v. lipid to 15–30% of non-protein energy provided by PN and cyclic

). The role of a limited lipid administration ( ) is also strengthened by reports of a beneficial effect of a fish-oil emulsion given at 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 when compared to traditional soy bean emulsions infused at 1–4 g·kg −1 ·d −1 ( – ). As a note of caution, the extent to which there is an overlap of cases reported in six separate publications of one group is unclear ( – , ). In a recent ESPGHAN position paper ( ) early EN limiting i. v. lipid to 15–30% of non-protein energy provided by PN and cyclic administration of PN once the patient is stable is recommended. The use of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and erythromycin has been reported to facilitate EN in premature infants on PN ( ). The authors of the ASPEN clinical guidelines analyzed seven publications on this issue and found a very low level of evidence for a beneficial role of UDCA in the treatment of PNAC ( ). They also analyzed the role of a multidisciplinary intestinal rehabilitation team in the management of IFALD and suggest to refer patients with PN-dependent intestinal failure to such a team conceding, however, a low level of evidence on this topic ( ). For the prevention of IFALD adults, the ESPEN guidelines ( ) recommend infection control, maintenance of oral and/or enteral intake, cycled PN ( ), avoidance of PN overfeeding and limiting the dose of soybean-oil based lipid to ≤ 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 ( ). 7.5 In adults / children, can special components (e.g. omega-3 FA) of the nutrition solution when compared to a standard nutrition solution improve/prevent a. biochemical signs of hepatocyte lesion, b. impaired liver function, c. abnormal liver histology, d. chronic liver disease? Recommendation 84 In case of PNAC in infants and children, lipid emulsions enriched with omega-3-fatty acids can be used. (BM) Grade of recommendation 0 – Strong consensus (100% agreement) Commentary Lipid emulsions containing fish oils as the triglyceride source were proposed to be protective in PNALD. This has been evaluated in a number of publications including cases, case series, or cohort data. In these reports a 100 % fish-oil emulsion was infused at a rate limited to 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 whereas the soy-bean emulsion was given at rates up to 4.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 and thus, it cannot be excluded that the quantity of lipid infused rather than its composition determined the observed improved outcome ( – , , ). In a retrospective analysis of 51 pediatric PNALD patients with cirrhosis the use of a fish-oil based lipid emulsion was accompanied by a resolution of cholestasis in 76 % ( ). A randomized controlled trial comparing a 100 % fish-oil emulsion with a soy-bean lipid emulsion both at a dose of 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 was terminated early because of an unexpectedly low incidence of PNAC ( ). No patient developed fatty acid deficiency and both regimens were well tolerated and safe. In a different approach, the reduction of soy-bean based lipid has been achieved by adding a fish-oil emulsion ( ), or using lipid emulsions consisting of a mixture of either soy-bean based lipid and medium-chained triglyceride MCT-lipid ( , ), or a mixture of a fish-oil emulsion and a soy-bean olive-oil emulsion ( ), or soy-bean based lipid and olive oil and MCT-lipid and fish-oil (SMOF emulsion) ( , – ). In randomized controlled trials comparing a SMOF emulsion with a soy-bean based emulsion the fish-oil containing SMOF emulsion proved to be safe and more effective in reducing bilirubin levels or oxidative stress ( , – ). In an analysis of 292 infants receiving more than one day of PN postoperatively, 31 infants reached a serum bilirubin > 100 µmol/L and 13 developed liver failure, whereas 86 (83 %) reaching a serum bilirubin > 33 µmol/L could be weaned off PN ( ). The authors question the routine use of a fish-oil emulsion in such a population outside of formal research protocols. These results again bring into focus the uncertainty in the diagnosis of IFALD, PNALD and PNAC ( , ) because cholestasis alone is not necessarily equivalent to liver injury and in this view PNAC may be seen as a component of PNALD. Both, the ASPEN guidelines paper on PNALD ( ) and the ESPGHAN position paper on intestinal failure ( ) conclude that currently there is no sound evidence favoring a specific lipid emulsion and that soy-bean based lipid infusion should be limited in hyper-bilirubinemia. Despite promising observations, the role of fish-oil emulsions needs to be established in randomized controlled trials. The authors of the ASPEN guideline delineate four questions to be answered ( ): Will a long-term reduction in soy-based fat emulsion dose to ≤ 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d

in this view PNAC may be seen as a component of PNALD. Both, the ASPEN guidelines paper on PNALD ( ) and the ESPGHAN position paper on intestinal failure ( ) conclude that currently there is no sound evidence favoring a specific lipid emulsion and that soy-bean based lipid infusion should be limited in hyper-bilirubinemia. Despite promising observations, the role of fish-oil emulsions needs to be established in randomized controlled trials. The authors of the ASPEN guideline delineate four questions to be answered ( ): Will a long-term reduction in soy-based fat emulsion dose to ≤ 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 result in adequate growth and neurological development, and will essential fatty acid deficiency be prevented? Is a fish-oil emulsion more effective than an equivalently dosed soy-based emulsion at preventing PNALD, promoting neurological development? What is the incidence of essential fatty acid deficiency if the low dose is given over a long duration, and how should essential fatty acid deficiency be tracked in these individuals? Is SMOF given at conventional lipid doses effective at preventing the development of PNALD while optimizing growth and development over the long term? Recommendation 85 In adults with suspected PNALD, lipid emulsions with a reduced n6/n3 ratio can be used. (BM) Grade of recommendation 0 – Strong consensus (92% agreement) Commentary In adults, less data is available regarding the effect of modifying quantity and/or composition of parenteral lipid on the course of PNALD. Limiting soy-bean based lipid to ≤ 1.0 g·kg −1 ·d −1 has been suggested also in adults ( ). The exchange of soy-bean based lipid by a 100 % fish-oil emulsion has been reported effective in two cases of PNALD ( , ). In a series of 15 patients, the addition of a fish-oil emulsion to a soy-bean based lipid emulsion was associated with reversal of biopsy proven PNALD ( ). In one case, the use of a fish-oil emulsion together with an olive-oil based PN regimen was associated with a reduction in liver steatosis and inflammation ( ). Taken together, more data are needed before the routine use of fish-oil containing fat emulsions can be recommended for the treatment of PNALD ( ).

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Acute pancreatitis during pregnancy and the early postpartum period is a rare but clinically important condition, with an estimated incidence of 1–3 cases per 10,000 pregnancies [ , ]. Despite its low frequency, moderate to severe disease may be associated with substantial maternal morbidity and, in selected cases, foetal compromise [ ]. Historically, maternal and foetal mortality rates were reported to be as high as 30–60%; however, advances in diagnostic imaging, intensive care, and multidisciplinary management have markedly improved outcomes over recent decades [ , ]. The temporal distribution of APIP is characteristic, with most cases occurring in the third trimester or in the early postpartum period [ , ]. During this phase, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and ileus may overlap with obstetric, surgical, or postoperative conditions, particularly following caesarean delivery, increasing the risk of delayed diagnosis. From an obstetric anaesthesia perspective, APIP represents a challenging perioperative condition that often requires early anaesthesiology involvement for haemodynamic stabilisation, analgesia, and critical care triage. Pregnancy-related cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic adaptations modify the systemic inflammatory response and may mask early organ dysfunction. Anaesthesiologists are frequently involved in analgesia, haemodynamic stabilisation, airway management, and ICU triage; nevertheless, these aspects remain underrepresented in many reviews focusing primarily on obstetric or gastroenterological perspectives. An anaesthesiology-centred narrative is therefore clinically relevant. 2. Methods 2.1. Study Design and Scope No specific instruments, proprietary software, or commercial agents requiring manufacturer identification were used in this study. The manuscript is based on a narrative synthesis of previously published literature. Standard bibliographic databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase) were used for literature retrieval; these are publicly accessible platforms and do not have fixed version numbers. Therefore, company names, addresses, and software version numbers are not applicable. 2.2. Literature Identification and Selection Relevant literature was identified through targeted searches of the PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase databases, focusing on publications addressing acute pancreatitis in pregnancy, postpartum pancreatitis, obstetric anaesthesia, pain management, and intensive care management. Priority was given to clinical studies, reviews, consensus guidelines, and landmark articles published in peer-reviewed journals. The reference lists of key articles were also manually screened to identify additional relevant sources. 2.3. Data Synthesis and Clinical Framework The retrieved evidence was synthesised thematically, with emphasis on epidemiology, aetiology, diagnostic strategies, severity assessment, and perioperative management. Anaesthesiology- and ICU-specific considerations—including analgesic strategies, fluid resuscitation, haemodynamic monitoring, respiratory support, and criteria for intensive care admission—were integrated into a pragmatic, severity-adapted management framework. The available evidence was interpreted in the context of pregnancy-related physiological adaptations and postpartum surgical stress. 2.4. Ethical Considerations This article is based on previously published data and anonymised clinical experience. No new experimental interventions were performed; therefore, formal ethical approval was not required. 3. Aetiology and Pathophysiology Gallstone disease is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis during pregnancy, accounting for more than half of reported cases [ , ]. Hormonal influences, particularly progesterone, alter bile composition and gallbladder motility, promoting biliary stasis and gallstone formation. These mechanisms are most pronounced in late pregnancy, corresponding with the peak incidence of APIP [ ]. Hypertriglyceridaemia represents the second most frequent aetiology and is associated with a higher likelihood of severe disease [ , ]. Pregnancy-related metabolic changes may increase plasma triglyceride levels two- to threefold due to reduced lipoprotein lipase activity and enhanced hepatic lipid synthesis. The risk of pancreatitis rises substantially when triglyceride levels exceed 500 mg/dL, particularly in patients with obesity or pre-existing dyslipidaemia [ ]. Less common causes include drug-induced pancreatitis, alcohol consumption, and idiopathic disease. In the early postpartum period, surgical stress and inflammatory activation following caesarean delivery may contribute to disease onset in selected cases [ , ]. Regardless of aetiology, premature pancreatic enzyme activation initiates a local inflammatory cascade that may progress to systemic inflammatory response syndrome and multiorgan failure. Systemic inflammatory response and mediator activation play a key role in disease progression [ , , ]. 4. Diagnosis and Imaging Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis in pregnancy relies on the same core criteria as in the non-pregnant population [ , , ]. Clinical presentation, however, may be atypical, particularly in late gestation or in the immediate postoperative period following caesarean delivery. Differential diagnostic considerations are particularly important in pregnant and early postpartum patients, where multiple obstetric and non-obstetric conditions may mimic acute pancreatitis. Key distinguishing features are summarised in . 5. Severity Assessment and Prognosis Severity stratification is a cornerstone of clinical decision-making in acute pancreatitis, guiding monitoring intensity, level of care, and therapeutic strategy. Severity classification and complication definitions are based on the Revised Atlanta Classification, which is summarised in [ ]. 6. Perioperative and Intensive Care Management Algorithm in APIP Acute pancreatitis in pregnancy and the early postpartum period (APIP) requires structured, severity-adapted perioperative and critical care management. Pregnancy-related physiological changes and the frequent overlap with obstetric or postoperative conditions

patients, where multiple obstetric and non-obstetric conditions may mimic acute pancreatitis. Key distinguishing features are summarised in . 5. Severity Assessment and Prognosis Severity stratification is a cornerstone of clinical decision-making in acute pancreatitis, guiding monitoring intensity, level of care, and therapeutic strategy. Severity classification and complication definitions are based on the Revised Atlanta Classification, which is summarised in [ ]. 6. Perioperative and Intensive Care Management Algorithm in APIP Acute pancreatitis in pregnancy and the early postpartum period (APIP) requires structured, severity-adapted perioperative and critical care management. Pregnancy-related physiological changes and the frequent overlap with obstetric or postoperative conditions may delay diagnosis and obscure early organ dysfunction. Anaesthesiologists therefore play a central role in early triage, haemodynamic stabilisation, analgesia, respiratory support, and the timely escalation of care. 6.1. Initial Assessment and Triage Early clinical assessment should focus on identifying systemic inflammatory response and early organ dysfunction. Particular attention should be paid to haemodynamic instability, hypoxaemia, oliguria, and altered mental status, which may be masked by pregnancy- and postpartum-related physiological adaptations. Laboratory evaluation should include pancreatic enzymes, inflammatory markers, renal and hepatic function tests, and serum triglyceride levels. Severity stratification should be performed early using the Revised Atlanta Classification [ ]. Given the potential for rapid deterioration, a lower threshold for high-dependency or intensive care unit (ICU) admission is recommended in pregnant and postpartum patients, particularly in the presence of persistent systemic inflammatory response, respiratory compromise, or increasing analgesic requirements. 6.2. Fluid Resuscitation and Haemodynamic Management Balanced crystalloids, particularly lactated Ringer’s solution, are preferred over normal saline due to their favourable effects on acid–base balance and systemic inflammation [ ]. Haemodynamic targets should be individualised, with close monitoring of mean arterial pressure, urine output, serum lactate, and dynamic indices of fluid responsiveness when available. Invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring should be considered in patients with haemodynamic instability or severe disease. Vasopressor support may be required in refractory hypotension and should be initiated early in an ICU setting. 6.3. Analgesia and Pain Management Effective pain control is essential in APIP management. Multimodal analgesia strategies are recommended, combining paracetamol, carefully titrated opioids, and neuraxial techniques when appropriate. Epidural analgesia may provide opioid-sparing pain relief, improve respiratory mechanics, and support haemodynamic stability. 6.4. Respiratory Support and ICU Admission Criteria Respiratory compromise may develop early due to pain-related hypoventilation, systemic inflammation, or fluid overload. Continuous pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas analysis should be used liberally. Supplemental oxygen should be initiated promptly, and non-invasive ventilation may be considered in selected cases. Indications for ICU admission include persistent organ failure lasting longer than 48 h, escalating oxygen requirements, haemodynamic instability, acute kidney injury, or suspected infected pancreatic necrosis. Early multidisciplinary involvement—including anaesthesiology, intensive care, obstetrics, gastroenterology, and surgery—is essential to optimise maternal outcomes. 6.5. Postpartum-Specific Considerations Analgesic strategies must consider breastfeeding safety, while nutritional planning should support maternal recovery and prevent metabolic deterioration. Early mobilisation, thromboprophylaxis, and vigilant monitoring for postoperative complications are integral components of care. 6.6. Interventional and Surgical Management During Pregnancy Biliary pancreatitis represents the most frequent aetiological subtype of APIP, and definitive management of the underlying cause is often required to prevent recurrence. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy is considered safe during pregnancy when performed by experienced teams with minimised fluoroscopy time and appropriate foetal shielding. ERCP is primarily indicated in cases of persistent biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or ongoing clinical deterioration despite conservative management. Available evidence suggests that therapeutic ERCP during pregnancy is associated with favourable maternal outcomes and low foetal complication rates when radiation exposure is carefully controlled [ ]. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is regarded as the definitive treatment for gallstone-related pancreatitis. Current data indicate that laparoscopic surgery can be performed safely during all trimesters, although the second trimester has traditionally been considered optimal due to lower risks of miscarriage and preterm labour. Early cholecystectomy following mild biliary pancreatitis may reduce recurrence risk and unplanned hospital readmissions. In cases of severe pancreatitis with persistent organ failure or necrotising disease, surgical or minimally invasive interventions should follow standard severity-based principles. Timing of intervention should be individualised and ideally postponed until the necrotic collection has become walled-off, unless sepsis or abdominal compartment syndrome mandates earlier action. Multidisciplinary coordination between obstetrics, surgery, gastroenterology, anaesthesiology, and intensive care teams is essential to optimise maternal and foetal safety. Key anaesthesiology- and intensive-care-specific considerations related to interventional and perioperative management are summarised in . 7. Discussion Recent predictive models, including nomogram-based approaches, have been proposed to improve early risk stratification in acute pancreatitis during pregnancy, although their clinical applicability remains to be validated in larger cohorts [ ]. A previously published postpartum case from our institution further illustrates the diagnostic challenges of acute pancreatitis following caesarean delivery [ ]. Building on this clinical observation, acute pancreatitis in pregnancy and the early postpartum period (APIP) represents a

anaesthesiology, and intensive care teams is essential to optimise maternal and foetal safety. Key anaesthesiology- and intensive-care-specific considerations related to interventional and perioperative management are summarised in . 7. Discussion Recent predictive models, including nomogram-based approaches, have been proposed to improve early risk stratification in acute pancreatitis during pregnancy, although their clinical applicability remains to be validated in larger cohorts [ ]. A previously published postpartum case from our institution further illustrates the diagnostic challenges of acute pancreatitis following caesarean delivery [ ]. Building on this clinical observation, acute pancreatitis in pregnancy and the early postpartum period (APIP) represents a uniquely complex clinical entity situated at the intersection of obstetric medicine, perioperative care, and critical illness. Although epidemiologically rare, APIP carries disproportionate clinical significance because of its diagnostic ambiguity, its potential for rapid deterioration, and the physiological vulnerability imposed by pregnancy-related adaptations. One of the central challenges in APIP is diagnostic delay, which frequently arises from symptom overlap with obstetric, surgical, and postoperative conditions. Abdominal pain, nausea, ileus, and haemodynamic variability are common in late pregnancy and following caesarean delivery, often obscuring early recognition of pancreatic inflammation. This diagnostic uncertainty is not merely a logistical concern but a pathophysiological hazard, as delayed diagnosis is strongly associated with increased disease severity, higher rates of organ failure, and prolonged maternal morbidity. The present review underscores that clinical vigilance and early biochemical evaluation remain critical determinants of outcome. The Revised Atlanta Classification [ ] (Banks et al., 2013) provides an essential framework for severity stratification; however, its application in pregnant patients warrants nuanced interpretation. Pregnancy induces profound cardiovascular, respiratory, and renal adaptations that may mask early indicators of systemic deterioration. Increased cardiac output, reduced systemic vascular resistance, and altered intravascular volume dynamics may transiently preserve macrocirculatory parameters despite evolving microcirculatory dysfunction. Similarly, reduced functional residual capacity and pregnancy-associated respiratory mechanics may accelerate hypoxaemia once pulmonary complications develop. Consequently, organ failure in APIP may manifest abruptly rather than progressively, supporting the rationale for a lower threshold for high-dependency monitoring and ICU admission. The present review provides an anaesthesiology-centred framework that integrates perioperative risk assessment, multimodal analgesia strategies, and critical care escalation pathways for pregnant and postpartum patients with acute pancreatitis. 8. Conclusions Acute pancreatitis in pregnancy and the early postpartum period remains a rare but clinically significant condition requiring heightened clinical awareness, particularly in the context of overlapping obstetric and postoperative presentations. Early recognition, timely severity stratification, and pregnancy-adapted diagnostic strategies are critical to prevent delayed intervention and progression to organ failure. Severity-adapted, multidisciplinary management represents the cornerstone of care, with anaesthesiology-led strategies playing a pivotal role in optimising analgesia, haemodynamic stability, respiratory support, and timely escalation to intensive care. Structured perioperative decision-making and early involvement of critical care teams may mitigate maternal morbidity and improve short-term outcomes. Close collaboration between obstetricians, anaesthesiologists, intensivists, gastroenterologists, and surgeons is essential to ensure coordinated care throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period. Future studies should focus on refining risk stratification tools and developing pregnancy-specific management pathways to further improve maternal safety in this vulnerable patient population.

chunks.content: Introduction The incidence of EC is steadily rising, particularly among elderly women, posing significant challenges for clinical management due to age-related comorbidities, aggressive tumor biology, and reduced treatment tolerance [ , ]. Advanced age is a well-established negative prognostic factor, often associated with higher recurrence rates and cancer-related mortality despite standard radical hysterectomy with lymph node assessment [ , ]. In line with geriatric oncology research, we defined “elderly” as age ≥ 65 years, which is a widely accepted threshold in both clinical trials and epidemiological studies of EC. This age cutoff is recommended by organizations such as the World Health Organization and is commonly used in geriatric oncology to identify patients at higher risk of functional decline, comorbidities, and treatment-related toxicity. Although alternative cutoffs (e.g., ≥ 70 or ≥ 75 years) exist, the age of 65 years represents a common benchmark for identifying patients with increased vulnerability to treatment-related toxicity and worse cancer outcomes. This heterogeneity in outcomes underscores the critical need for robust, readily available prognostic biomarkers to improve risk stratification and personalize postoperative management for elderly EC patients. The tumor microenvironment and host systemic response, including nutrition and systemic inflammation, are closely related to cancer progression and treatment outcomes [ , ]. The GNRI, originally developed to assess nutritional risk in elderly hospitalized patients, has demonstrated significant prognostic value across various malignancies [ ]. This simple composite index, derived from serum albumin and body weight, reflects protein-energy malnutrition and skeletal muscle mass loss (sarcopenia), which are associated with worse treatment tolerance, increased postoperative complications, and impaired anti-tumor immunity [ ]. Concurrently, the systemic inflammatory response, mediated through various cytokines and cellular components, creates a favorable microenvironment for tumor proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastasis [ ]. Numerous inflammation-based scores have been studied in EC, but their prognostic values vary [ ]. More recently, the PIV has emerged as a novel, comprehensive biomarker that incorporates four key hematological parameters (neutrophils, platelets, monocytes, and lymphocytes) into a single formula, potentially providing a more complete reflection of the host’s immune-inflammatory status [ ]. Elevated PIV has demonstrated promising prognostic utility in several solid tumors, including colorectal, lung, and gastric cancers [ – ], with emerging evidence also supporting its prognostic value in other malignancies such as breast cancer and Merkel cell carcinoma [ , ]. Elderly EC patients represent a particularly vulnerable population where the interplay between malnutrition and inflammation is often pronounced and clinically significant [ ]. Age-related physiological decline, including anorexia of aging and sarcopenia, can predispose to nutritional deficiencies, while the tumor itself can promote a chronic inflammatory state through cytokine production and immune system modulation [ ]. This creates a vicious cycle that may accelerate disease progression and compromise treatment outcomes [ ]. Although GNRI and PIV have been studied independently in other cancer types, their combined prognostic power has not been investigated in EC, and their specific role in the elderly cohort remains largely unexplored [ – ]. Previous studies have typically examined nutritional and inflammatory markers separately, potentially overlooking their synergistic effect on patient outcomes [ ]. Furthermore, most existing prognostic models for EC have not adequately addressed the unique challenges faced by elderly patients, who often present with distinct tumor biology and host characteristics [ ]. This retrospective study, therefore, specifically aimed to address this gap by comprehensively evaluating the prognostic value of preoperative GNRI and PIV, both individually and in combination, in a cohort strictly limited to elderly patients (≥ 65 years) with EC undergoing radical surgery. While previous studies have reported the prognostic role of GNRI or PIV individually in various malignancies, including some gynecological cancers, few have focused specifically on the elderly EC population, in whom age-related physiological decline often leads to a pronounced interplay between malnutrition and chronic inflammation-a state sometimes termed “inflammaging”. We hypothesized that in this specific population, low GNRI and high PIV would be associated with aggressive clinicopathological characteristics and would independently predict worse overall survival, recurrence-free survival, and higher two-year recurrence rates. Furthermore, we postulated that the integration of these two host-specific factors would yield superior prognostic accuracy compared to using either marker alone or traditional tumor-centric factors, offering a simple, cost-effective, and clinically accessible tool for refining postoperative risk stratification and personalizing management strategies for this growing yet vulnerable patient subgroup. Materials and methods Study design and population We screened the medical records of elderly patients who underwent primary radical surgery for histologically proven EC at The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University between February 2021 and November 2023. The study protocol complied with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University Hospital (Approval No.: 2022 − 207; Date of Approval: May 27, 2022), and the informed consent

refining postoperative risk stratification and personalizing management strategies for this growing yet vulnerable patient subgroup. Materials and methods Study design and population We screened the medical records of elderly patients who underwent primary radical surgery for histologically proven EC at The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University between February 2021 and November 2023. The study protocol complied with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of The Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University Hospital (Approval No.: 2022 − 207; Date of Approval: May 27, 2022), and the informed consent was also obtained. The official ethics approval document is available upon request. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥ 65 years; (2) pathologically confirmed endometrial carcinoma; (3) receiving radical surgery, which in the context of this study refers to comprehensive surgical staging, defined as at minimum total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH + BSO), with or without pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph node assessment; (4) intact clinical records. Exclusion criteria included: (1) presence of synchronous other malignancies; (2) receipt of neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy prior to surgery; (3) receipt of any immunotherapy prior to surgery or during the study period; (4) active infection, autoimmune diseases, or chronic inflammatory conditions that could significantly affect inflammatory markers; (5) incomplete preoperative laboratory data (within one week before surgery) required for calculating GNRI and PIV; (6) incomplete clinicopathological or follow-up data. A final cohort of 156 patients was included in the analysis. To explore potential age-related heterogeneity, we performed a sensitivity analysis by stratifying patients into two age subgroups: 65–74 years ( n = 102) and ≥ 75 years ( n = 54). The prognostic impact of GNRI and PIV remained consistent across both subgroups (all P < 0.05), supporting the robustness of our findings within the defined elderly population. Additionally, we conducted subgroup analyses based on FIGO stage to evaluate the prognostic value of the combined GNRI-PIV stratification within early-stage (Stage I/II, n = 120) and advanced-stage (Stage III/IV, n = 36) disease. In the early-stage subgroup, patients with low GNRI/high PIV (Group 1) had significantly worse 3-year OS (61.5% vs. 92.9% in high GNRI/low PIV group, P < 0.001) and higher 2-year recurrence rate (57.1% vs. 10.2%, P < 0.001). Among advanced-stage patients, the combined GNRI-PIV groups also showed distinct survival outcomes (3-year OS: 41.7% in Group 1 vs. 77.8% in Group 4, P = 0.008). These results indicate that the combined GNRI-PIV model can further refine risk stratification within both early and advanced FIGO stages. Surgical procedures All patients underwent comprehensive surgical staging, which included at minimum a total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH + BSO). Pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) was performed in 150 patients (96.2%), and para-aortic lymph node dissection (PALND) was performed in 48 patients (30.8%) based on preoperative risk assessment and intraoperative findings. Sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping was utilized in 22 patients (14.1%). Surgical approach (open, laparoscopic, or robotic) was selected based on patient characteristics and surgeon preference. Omentectomy was not routinely performed unless there was clinical suspicion of extra-uterine disease. The median operative time was 180 min (IQR 150–210), and estimated blood loss was recorded. The distribution of surgical extent (lymph node assessment: PLND, PALND, SLN mapping) and surgical approach (minimally invasive vs. open) did not differ significantly across GNRI-PIV groups (all P > 0.05). Data collection and definitions Demographic, clinical, surgical, and pathological data were meticulously extracted from electronic medical records. Collected variables included age, BMI, FIGO stage (2009 criteria, as this was the institutional standard during the majority of the study period and ensures consistency in pathological reporting), histology, grade, myometrial invasion, LVSI, lymph node status, extent of lymph node assessment (PLND, PALND, SLN mapping), surgical approach (open, laparoscopic, robotic), and postoperative adjuvant treatments (categorized as none, radiotherapy alone, chemotherapy alone, or combined chemoradiotherapy). Preoperative laboratory data, including complete blood count with differential and serum albumin, were collected within one week before surgery. Data on postoperative adjuvant therapy (including radiotherapy, chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, or combinations thereof) were also collected. Adjuvant therapy decisions were made based on multidisciplinary tumor board recommendations considering pathological risk factors. Calculation of GNRI and PIV The GNRI was calculated using the following formula: GNRI = (1.489 × serum albumin [g/L]) + (41.7 × (current body weight [kg] / ideal body weight [kg])). As per the original GNRI methodology, if the ratio of current body weight to ideal body weight exceeded 1, it was set to 1 to avoid overestimating nutritional status in overweight or obese individuals [ ]. The ideal body weight was derived from the Lorentz formula for women: Ideal weight (kg) = Height (cm) − 100 - ((Height (cm) − 150) / 2.5). Based on the formula of PIV = (neutrophil count × platelet count × monocyte count) /

following formula: GNRI = (1.489 × serum albumin [g/L]) + (41.7 × (current body weight [kg] / ideal body weight [kg])). As per the original GNRI methodology, if the ratio of current body weight to ideal body weight exceeded 1, it was set to 1 to avoid overestimating nutritional status in overweight or obese individuals [ ]. The ideal body weight was derived from the Lorentz formula for women: Ideal weight (kg) = Height (cm) − 100 - ((Height (cm) − 150) / 2.5). Based on the formula of PIV = (neutrophil count × platelet count × monocyte count) / lymphocyte count, PIV was calculated. All blood cell counts were expressed as 10⁹/L. The resulting PIV is a unitless ratio, with higher values indicating a more pronounced pro-inflammatory and immunosuppressive state. Follow-up and endpoints Patients were followed according to institutional guidelines: quarterly for the first 2 years, semi-annually for the next 3 years, and annually thereafter. Physical examination, serum cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) testing, and imaging were performed during the follow-up as clinically indicated. The primary endpoints were OS and RFS. Secondary endpoints included two-year recurrence rates. The 3-year OS endpoint was selected because it represents a clinically meaningful medium-term survival benchmark in endometrial carcinoma, especially in elderly patients with competing risks of mortality. The 2-year recurrence endpoint was chosen specifically to focus on early recurrence patterns, which are particularly relevant for aggressive disease biology and have been associated with worse long-term outcomes in endometrial carcinoma. Early recurrence (within 24 months) often reflects more aggressive tumor behavior and may necessitate intensified surveillance or adjuvant strategies. This endpoint differs from RFS in that it is a binary outcome (recurrence yes/no within 24 months) and does not incorporate death events, providing a distinct measure of early tumor aggressiveness. RFS referred to the interval from surgery to first recurrence or death from any cause. The interval from surgery to death from any cause was defined for OS. Event-free patients were censored at their last follow-up. The follow-up data were updated until March 2025, providing a minimum potential follow-up time of 16 months for all patients. Patients without an event (recurrence or death) at the last contact before March 2025 were censored at that date. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS 26.0 and R 4.2.0. Categorical data are presented as n (%) and analyzed with chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range based on distribution normality, and compared using Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test as appropriate. The 3-year OS and 2-year recurrence endpoints were selected as clinically meaningful benchmarks for medium-term survival and early recurrence in this elderly cohort, respectively. To determine optimal prognostic cutoffs for GNRI and PIV for predicting 3-year OS while appropriately handling censored survival data, we performed time-dependent ROC analysis at 36 months using the “timeROC” package in R, with the cutpoint selected based on the maximum Youden index. Patients were subsequently stratified into high and low groups based on these cutoffs (GNRI: 97.8, PIV: 292.3). It should be noted that these cutoffs were derived from the present cohort and are considered exploratory, requiring validation in external populations. Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test. The proportional hazards assumption was tested using Schoenfeld residuals and was satisfied. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify independent prognostic factors. Variables with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis for the respective endpoint were considered for inclusion. The final multivariate model for each endpoint was constructed by including the two primary biomarkers (GNRI and PIV) and the most clinically relevant factors (FIGO stage and lymph node metastasis). To account for potential confounding, adjuvant therapy (categorized as none, radiotherapy alone, chemotherapy alone, or combined chemoradiotherapy) was forced into all multivariate models. No significant interaction was found between adjuvant therapy type and GNRI/PIV status regarding OS or RFS ( P for interaction > 0.05). The stability of the multivariate model coefficients was internally assessed using 1000 bootstrap resamples. Biomarker performance was compared using time-dependent ROC analysis with the DeLong test, and the discriminatory power of the combined model was assessed using Harrell’s C-index. All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Most patients had endometrioid histology (90.4%), early-stage (FIGO I/II) disease (76.9%), and grade 1–2 tumors (73.7%). Among the 15 (9.6%) patients with non-endometrioid histology (including serous, clear cell, carcinosarcoma, and mixed types), the distribution across GNRI-PIV groups was as follows: Group 1 (Low GNRI/High PIV): 7 (18.4% of Group 1), Group 2: 4 (11.8%), Group 3: 2 (6.3%), Group 4: 2 (3.8%). This distribution suggests a trend toward more aggressive histologies in the high-risk biomarker group, though the numbers are small for formal subgroup analysis. The optimal cutoffs for 3-year OS prediction were GNRI: 97.8 (sensitivity 77.1%, specificity 72.7%) and PIV: 292.3 (sensitivity 74.3%, specificity 70.2%), determined by time-dependent ROC analysis at 36 months. Based on these, 72 patients (46.2%) were classified into the low GNRI group and 70 patients (44.9%) into the high PIV group. The associations between clinicopathological characteristics and GNRI/PIV status are summarized in Table . Patients with low GNRI were significantly older, had lower BMI, and had more aggressive tumor features, including advanced FIGO stage, higher tumor grade, positive lymph node metastasis, and greater frequency of LVSI (all P < 0.05). Similarly, a high PIV was significantly associated with advanced stage, lower BMI, older age, higher grade, and lymph node metastasis (all P < 0.05). The association between high PIV and deeper myometrial invasion (≥ 50%) showed a trend but did not reach statistical significance ( P = 0.078). Regarding treatment-related factors, adjuvant therapy was administered to 102 patients (65.4%): radiotherapy alone in 45 patients (28.8%), chemotherapy alone in 32 patients (20.5%), and combined chemoradiotherapy in 25 patients (16.0%). Pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) was performed in 150 patients (96.2%), para-aortic lymph node dissection (PALND) in 48 (30.8%), and sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping in 22 (14.1%). Minimally invasive surgery (laparoscopic or robotic) was performed in 118 patients (75.6%). The administration of adjuvant therapy, the extent of lymph node assessment (PLND, PALND, SLN mapping), and the surgical approach did not differ significantly between the low and high GNRI or PIV groups (all P > 0.05, Table ). Survival outcomes The patients were followed up for a median duration of 28 months (range, 6–56 months). By the last follow-up (March 2025), 35 (22.4%) patients had died and 45 (28.8%) had experienced recurrence or death. KM analysis revealed that patients with low GNRI had significantly worse OS (3-year OS: 65.3% vs. 89.3%, P < 0.001) and RFS (3-year RFS: 60.8% vs. 82.1%, P < 0.001) compared to those with high GNRI. Similarly, patients with high PIV had significantly poorer OS (3-year OS: 67.1% vs. 86.0%, P < 0.001) and RFS (3-year RFS: 62.9% vs. 80.2%, P = 0.001) than those with low PIV. To further evaluate the synergistic prognostic effect, patients were stratified into four groups based on their GNRI and PIV status: Group 1 (low GNRI and high PIV, n = 38), Group 2 (low GNRI and low PIV, n = 34), Group 3 (high GNRI and high PIV, n = 32), and Group 4 (high GNRI and low PIV, n = 52). Patients with low GNRI had a significantly higher 2-year recurrence rate compared to those with high GNRI (42.6% vs. 16.7%, P < 0.001, derived from Kaplan-Meier estimates). Significant variables ( P < 0.1) were incorporated into the multivariate Cox model. Multivariate analysis confirmed that both low GNRI (OS: HR = 2.42, 95% CI: 1.58–3.70, P < 0.001; RFS: HR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.43–3.24, P < 0.001) and high PIV (OS: HR = 2.18, 95% CI: 1.43–3.32, P < 0.001; RFS: HR = 1.94, 95% CI: 1.30–2.90, P = 0.001) remained independent predictors of poor OS and RFS after adjusting for other clinicopathological factors and the modality of adjuvant therapy (categorized as none, radiotherapy alone, chemotherapy alone, or combined chemoradiotherapy). The details are listed in Table . Combined prognostic value of GNRI and PIV The baseline characteristics of the four groups stratified by GNRI and PIV are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. Patients in Group 1 (low GNRI / high PIV) were the oldest, had the lowest BMI, and exhibited the most aggressive tumor features, including the highest rates of advanced FIGO stage (52.6%), grade 3 tumors (47.4%), lymph node metastasis (42.1%), LVSI (47.4%), and deep myometrial invasion (57.9%). In contrast, Group 4 (high GNRI / low PIV) had the most favorable profile, with the youngest age, highest BMI, and lowest rates of adverse pathological features. Groups 2 and 3 showed intermediate characteristics. The prognostic performance of the combined GNRI-PIV model was evaluated using ROC analysis. For predicting 3-year OS, the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.74–0.88), which was higher than that of GNRI alone (AUC = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.63–0.79; P = 0.032) or PIV alone (AUC = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.61–0.77; P = 0.018) (Fig. ). First, a baseline clinical model was built using well-established prognostic factors: age (≥ 75 vs. <75), FIGO stage (III/IV vs. I/II), tumor grade (3 vs. 1–2), lymph node metastasis (yes vs. no), and lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI; yes vs. no). For 3-year OS, this baseline model yielded a Harrell’s C-index of 0.72 (95% CI: 0.65–0.79). Subsequently, GNRI (dichotomized by the cutoff of 97.8) and PIV (dichotomized by the cutoff of 292.3) were added to the baseline model, resulting in a significantly improved C-index of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.73–0.85). To assess model stability, we performed 10-fold cross-validation, which yielded a mean AUC of 0.79 (standard deviation, SD = 0.03) for the combined model, indicating robust internal validity. The detailed results of these incremental value analyses are summarized in Table . Similarly, for 3-year RFS, the combined model showed an AUC of 0.78, outperforming the individual markers (GNRI AUC = 0.72, P = 0.041; PIV AUC = 0.70, P = 0.025). The Harrell’s C-index for the combined model for OS prediction was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.73–0.85), further validating its robust discriminatory power. The incremental prognostic value of adding GNRI and PIV to a baseline clinical model (including age, FIGO stage, grade, LNM, and LVSI) is summarized in Table . For 3-year OS, the addition of GNRI and PIV to the baseline clinical model led to a statistically significant improvement in the C-index (ΔC-index = 0.07, P = 0.012), IDI (0.09, P = 0.005), and NRI (0.42, P < 0.001). Similar improvements were observed for 3-year RFS (ΔC-index = 0.06, P = 0.019; IDI = 0.08, P = 0.008; NRI = 0.38, P < 0.001). These analyses confirm that GNRI and PIV provide significant prognostic information beyond that offered by traditional clinicopathological factors alone. To further integrate traditional clinicopathological factors, we constructed a combined model incorporating FIGO stage (I/II vs. III/IV), GNRI, and PIV (termed the “FIGO + GNRI + PIV” model). For predicting 3-year OS, this integrated model achieved an AUC of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.79–0.91), which was significantly higher than that of the model based on FIGO stage alone (AUC = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.62–0.78; DeLong test P < 0.001) and also superior to the “GNRI + PIV” combined model (AUC = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.74–0.88; DeLong test P = 0.039). For 3-year RFS, the “FIGO + GNRI + PIV” model achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.76–0.88), which was significantly better than the FIGO-stage-alone model (AUC = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.60–0.76; P < 0.001, DeLong test) and showed a trend towards improvement compared to the “GNRI + PIV” model (AUC = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.71–0.85; P = 0.067, DeLong test). Discussion Our study is the first to comprehensively evaluate the combined prognostic role of preoperative GNRI and PIV exclusively in a cohort of elderly (≥ 65 years) patients with EC undergoing radical surgery. Our findings robustly demonstrate that both biomarkers, reflecting distinct yet interconnected domains of host status (nutrition and systemic inflammation), are powerful independent predictors of OS, RFS, and early recurrence in this vulnerable population. Crucially, the novel combination of these easily accessible, preoperative markers provided superior risk stratification compared to clinicopathological factors alone, highlighting their potential to augment existing prognostic models. The core innovation of this research lies in demonstrating that a combined host-factor model, readily derivable from routine preoperative data, effectively stratifies risk specifically within the challenging context of geriatric EC. The prognostic significance of GNRI in our study aligns with growing evidence linking malnutrition to poor cancer outcomes [ , , ]. In elderly EC patients, nutritional status assumes even greater importance due to age-related physiological changes, including sarcopenia and anorexia of aging [ , ]. Our results extend previous findings by specifically focusing on the elderly population and demonstrating that GNRI not only predicts long-term survival but also early recurrence rates. The mechanisms underlying this association are multifactorial, including reduced treatment tolerance, impaired immune function, and metabolic alterations that may promote tumor progression [ , ]. The simplicity of GNRI calculation, based on routinely available parameters (albumin and weight), enhances its clinical applicability as a practical tool for identifying high-risk elderly EC patients who might benefit from preoperative nutritional assessment and targeted interventions, a consideration of particular importance in a population prone to sarcopenia and anorexia of aging. Similarly, the independent prognostic value of PIV underscores the critical role of systemic inflammation in EC progression. PIV integrates key cellular components of the immune-inflammatory response: neutrophils and platelets that promote angiogenesis and metastasis; monocytes that differentiate into tumor-associated macrophages fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment; and lymphocytes

The simplicity of GNRI calculation, based on routinely available parameters (albumin and weight), enhances its clinical applicability as a practical tool for identifying high-risk elderly EC patients who might benefit from preoperative nutritional assessment and targeted interventions, a consideration of particular importance in a population prone to sarcopenia and anorexia of aging. Similarly, the independent prognostic value of PIV underscores the critical role of systemic inflammation in EC progression. PIV integrates key cellular components of the immune-inflammatory response: neutrophils and platelets that promote angiogenesis and metastasis; monocytes that differentiate into tumor-associated macrophages fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment; and lymphocytes that are crucial for anti-tumor immunity [ , ]. An elevated PIV thus reflects enhanced pro-tumor inflammation and suppressed anti-tumor immunity. Our findings are consistent with studies in other malignancies [ – , ] and suggest that PIV may represent a more comprehensive indicator of the host’s immune status compared to simpler ratios like NLR or PLR, although direct comparative studies are warranted. The most significant contribution of our study is the demonstration of a powerful synergistic effect between nutritional status (GNRI) and systemic inflammation (PIV). The combined biomarkers effectively categorized patients into four distinct risk groups with markedly different survival outcomes and recurrence patterns. Patients with concurrent malnutrition (low GNRI) and high systemic inflammation (high PIV) exhibited the worst prognosis, with a strikingly high two-year recurrence rate of 65.8% and significantly inferior OS and RFS. This finding highlights the vicious cycle between these two conditions, often referred to as “inflammaging” and malnutrition-sarcopenia syndrome in the elderly [ , ]. From a pathophysiological perspective, malnutrition (reflected by low GNRI) leads to muscle wasting, reduced protein synthesis, and impaired immune cell function, while systemic inflammation (high PIV) promotes a pro-tumor microenvironment through cytokine release (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α), angiogenesis, and suppression of anti-tumor lymphocytes. Together, they create a state of chronic immune suppression and metabolic dysregulation that facilitates tumor progression, metastasis, and early recurrence. This pathological interplay can lead to functional decline, increased treatment toxicity, and accelerated disease progression through multiple mechanisms, including enhanced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired tissue repair capacity [ , ]. Conversely, patients with good nutritional status and low inflammation (high GNRI/low PIV) demonstrated excellent outcomes, with a two-year recurrence rate of 9.6% and the most favorable long-term survival. Interestingly, patients in Group 3 (high GNRI/high PIV) exhibited an even lower early recurrence rate of 3.1%, suggesting that good nutritional status may profoundly mitigate the impact of systemic inflammation on early disease control, a hypothesis warranting further investigation. This suggests that a robust host defense mechanism, characterized by adequate nutritional reserves and balanced immune function, may effectively contain tumor progression even in elderly patients. The identification of this low-risk subgroup is particularly clinically relevant, as it might allow for treatment de-escalation strategies to avoid overtreatment and preserve quality of life in this vulnerable population, especially for those with early-stage disease. The superior prognostic performance of the combined GNRI-PIV model, as evidenced by higher AUC values in ROC analysis and high Harrell’s C-index, underscores its potential clinical utility. Critically, our incremental value analyses demonstrated that adding GNRI and PIV to a model based on established clinical factors (age, FIGO stage, grade, LNM, LVSI) significantly improved risk stratification, as reflected by the increase in C-index, IDI, and NRI (Table ). This composite model outperformed not only individual markers but also traditional prognostic factors, suggesting that it captures essential aspects of the host-tumor interaction that are not fully reflected by conventional staging systems. The integration of nutritional and inflammatory assessment provides a more holistic view of the patient’s biological status, which is especially valuable in elderly cancer patients where host factors significantly influence treatment outcomes [ , ]. Our findings have important clinical implications. The preoperative assessment of GNRI and PIV is inexpensive, reproducible, and based on routine blood tests and anthropometric measurements. This combination could be easily integrated into clinical practice to improve risk stratification for elderly EC patients. As a hypothesis-generating perspective derived from our retrospective data, the GNRI-PIV model may help generate testable hypotheses for future risk-adapted strategies. While these concepts require rigorous validation, we posit that for high-risk patients (low GNRI/high PIV), future prospective trials could investigate the potential benefit of interventions such as preoperative nutritional optimization, physical prehabilitation, or intensified adjuvant regimens. For low-risk patients (high GNRI/low PIV), the hypothesis of de-escalating adjuvant therapy or follow-up intensity to reduce treatment burden without compromising oncologic safety could also be explored. We must underscore that all these potential strategies are speculative, derived from an observational study, and must be prospectively tested in well-designed clinical trials before any change to standard practice can be contemplated. Several limitations of this study warrant acknowledgment. Firstly, its retrospective and single-center design introduces potential selection bias. Secondly, the sample size, though reasonable,
