No significant difference was found between single versus multiple surgery participants (t = 0.53, df = 58, p = 0.60) but weight-unstable participants were significantly less likely to reconsider bariatric surgery compared to weight-stable participants (chi-square = 5.19, p = 0.023, df = 1). 3.7 Encountered barriers and peer advice presents reported postoperative encountered barriers and advices for peers at the beginning of the bariatric journey. The encountered barriers were categorized into eating and drinking, physical, psychological and social domains, overlapping with expectations. Two-third of all participants provided peer advices ranging from strong recommendations to cautionary guidance not to start a bariatric route. Most frequently advised was gathering comprehensive information from multiple sources regarding potential postoperative consequences. Additional recommendations highlighted awareness of emotional eating's impact, the importance of social support and necessity of dietary guideline adherence. Participants emphasized that bariatric surgery should be viewed as a facilitating tool for weight loss rather than a complete solution. They stressed that long-term success requires permanent lifestyle modifications. Many participants wanted prospective patients to understand that surgery is not a 'quick fix' but rather an intervention that requires sustained personal effort and commitment to achieve and maintain results. Some participants reported loneliness due to lack of understanding from family and friends regarding their surgical decision and insufficient emotional support during the postoperative period, leaving them feeling isolated in their bariatric journey. 4 Discussion The core objective of this study was to elicit patients' retrospective perspectives on their bariatric surgical trajectory and document their current and historical status across multiple long-term postoperative outcome domains, irrespective of surgical procedure. 4.1 Weight loss and weight stability After 19 years, mean weight loss was 33% with BMI reduction of 16 points and EWL of 61.2%. Individual variability was substantial, ranging from 150 kg weight loss to 20 kg weight gain. These findings align with limited long-term studies beyond 10 years reporting 14% weight loss after LAGB, 25% after gastric bypass, and 16% after VBG, with EWL ranging from 27 to 69% across procedures [ , ]. A 20-year LAGB study reported mean weight loss of 22% (30.1 kg) and BMI reduction of 10.6 points [ ]. Outcome variability has been attributed to surgical procedure, postoperative duration, and eating behaviors [ ]. Weight stability was reported by more than half of the participants and was associated with greater weight loss and satisfaction. Conversely, weight-unstable participants demonstrated less weight loss and reduced satisfaction. To our knowledge, no previous study examined persistence of weight instability after surgery. The weight instability findings require replication but may reflect persistent preoperative patterns. Literature primarily focuses on postoperative weight regain, which remains a concern even with contemporary procedures [ ]. Approximately 20% of patients experience over 15% body weight regain within 5 years, with 10-year data indicating mean regain of 36% (range 12–71%). In this study, 6.5% of participants regained to preoperative weight, defined as ≤5% from baseline. Weight regain to nearly preoperative levels occurred in 3.3% of LRYGB, 12.5% of sleeve gastrectomy, and 36% of LAGB patients at five years [ ]. Patients experienced weight regain as unexpected. They reported shame, discouragement, and frustration [ ]. 4.2 Surgical procedures and reoperation rate Most participants underwent LAGB or VBG, procedures now obsolete or less common [ ]. LAGB has declined despite fewer side effects, while VBG has been abandoned due to high failure and complication rates [ ]. In the present data, contemporary procedures as LSG and LRYGB [ ] were underrepresented. However, the examined aspects were expected to be transferable across surgical techniques since all patients face fundamental challenges of living with a surgically altered digestive system. Over half of participants underwent second or third procedures. Reoperations are common across all procedures, with rates varying by type and postoperative duration [ ]. LAGB 10-year reoperation rates ranged from 8 to 78% [ ], while LRYGB rates ranged from 8 to 64% [ , , ]. In this study, additional surgeries yielded no significant extra weight loss, with single-surgery participants demonstrating comparable outcomes. These results align with findings that reoperations five years post-surgery did not significantly impact weight loss or comorbidity remission [ ]. Preoperative counseling regarding realistic reoperation expectations is warranted. 4.3 Health behaviors and dietary guideline adherence Behaviors were classified as healthy (H), recommended for optimal outcomes or unhealthy (U) associated with increased risks. Percentages reflected actual patient-reported behaviors, not achievement of recommendations. Reported healthy behaviors were: regular meals, portion control and control regarding snacking between meals. Reported unhealthy behaviors were: meal skipping, uncontrolled eating, evening eating, alcohol consumption, and inadequate vitamin supplementation, mirroring our previous study, a cross-sectional cohort examining patient-reported outcomes approximately 5 years after bariatric surgery [ ]. Adopting healthy postoperative behaviors

weight loss or comorbidity remission [ ]. Preoperative counseling regarding realistic reoperation expectations is warranted. 4.3 Health behaviors and dietary guideline adherence Behaviors were classified as healthy (H), recommended for optimal outcomes or unhealthy (U) associated with increased risks. Percentages reflected actual patient-reported behaviors, not achievement of recommendations. Reported healthy behaviors were: regular meals, portion control and control regarding snacking between meals. Reported unhealthy behaviors were: meal skipping, uncontrolled eating, evening eating, alcohol consumption, and inadequate vitamin supplementation, mirroring our previous study, a cross-sectional cohort examining patient-reported outcomes approximately 5 years after bariatric surgery [ ]. Adopting healthy postoperative behaviors remained challenging for a substantial proportion of participants. Both studies documented persistent unhealthy eating behaviors and vitamin supplementation non-adherence in approximately one-third of patients, demonstrating these represent chronic challenges requiring sustained intervention rather than temporary postoperative adaptation issues that resolve spontaneously. Literature identifies uncontrolled eating as a primary factor in suboptimal weight loss and regain after surgery [ ]. Post-surgery patients must modify eating patterns and adhere to dietary guidelines throughout their lifespan to optimize outcomes [ , ]. Consistent with other studies, unhealthy eating behaviors including uncontrolled eating and binge eating disorders persisted. Nearly one-fifth of postoperative patients with uncontrolled eating met food addiction criteria [ ]. Research demonstrates reduced energy intake with high dietary adherence during the first two years [ , ], with eating primarily motivated by physical rather than emotional factors [ , , ]. However, within five years, emotional and unrestricted eating increased [ ], and after 10 years, reduced weight loss correlated with uncontrolled eating [ ]. In the preoperative phase, formal DSM eating disorder diagnoses (Bulimia Nervosa, Binge Eating Disorder) were exclusion criteria for bariatric surgery. Therefore, no participants had diagnosed eating disorders at the time of surgery. However, subthreshold binge eating behaviors, not meeting full diagnostic criteria, were not exclusionary. Nighttime eating (5%) and binge eating (17%) were relatively uncommon but may impede weight loss. Notably, binge eating prevalence decreased substantially from preoperative levels 55%–17% at 19 years. This reduction is particularly meaningful given that formal DSM eating disorder diagnoses (Bulimia Nervosa, Binge Eating Disorder) were exclusion criteria for bariatric surgery during the preoperative screening period. However, subthreshold binge eating behaviors not meeting full diagnostic criteria were not exclusionary, explaining the high preoperative prevalence. Previous research reported nighttime eating prevalence of 6–8% up to eight years postoperatively, associated with increasing BMI, with 15–20% of nighttime eaters meeting binge eating disorder criteria [ ]. These patient-centered findings highlight the importance of enhanced focus on long-term behavioral patterns. 4.4 Vitamin supplementation Vitamin supplementation is a healthy recommended behavior to prevent adverse health consequences including nutritional deficiencies [ ]. However, two-thirds of participants actually adhered to this recommendation, with one-third demonstrating unhealthy non-adherence, a concerning finding requiring clinical attention. Surgical techniques differentially affect nutrient absorption, potentially causing anemia, ataxia, hair loss, Wernicke encephalopathy [ ] or increased fracture risk [ ]. It has been shown that nutritional deficiencies occur in 30–70% of bariatric surgery patients as a result of reduced consumption or absorption [ ]. During the first year after surgery, studies indicated moderate to high vitamin adherence [ , ] but over time, vitamin A and folate deficiencies increased [ ]. After 17 years, an increased risk for anemia has been documented [ ]. Postoperative monitoring remains critical [ , , , ], even after 19 years. 4.5 Alcohol Over half of participants reported alcohol abstinence, while others reported occasional or frequent alcohol consumption. Postoperative alcohol avoidance is recommended due to potential B vitamin deficiencies and high caloric content [ ]. Literature shows initial less alcohol consumption within the first two years after surgery but increased consumption thereafter, particularly among men [ ]. Alcohol dependency risk has been observed compared to non-surgical controls [ ], especially following RYGB whereas sleeve gastrectomy, potentially reflecting altered reward circuits or symptom substitution [ ]. 4.6 Expectations and satisfaction Approximately half of participants reported congruence between preoperative expectations and postoperative outcomes; the remainder experienced outcomes exceeding or falling short across domains including weight loss, complications, and health status. In literature, patients often view surgery as a definitive solution, expecting unrealistic superior outcomes regarding weight loss magnitude. Beliefs as surgery will "solve my problems," "enhance appearance," or "guarantee success" are common and negatively influence postoperative outcomes, contributing to frustration and psychological decompensation [ ]. This study confirms that expectation-outcome discrepancies correlate with reduced satisfaction and decreased willingness to undergo surgery again. Addressing unrealistic expectations in the preoperative phase is recommended [ ]. Almost 80% would reconsider surgery, with satisfaction independent of weight loss or reoperation rate but significantly associated with weight stability and expectation-outcome congruence. This pattern aligns with long-term literature showing no association between satisfaction and absolute weight loss, underscoring the multifaceted nature of postoperative satisfaction [ ,

surgery will "solve my problems," "enhance appearance," or "guarantee success" are common and negatively influence postoperative outcomes, contributing to frustration and psychological decompensation [ ]. This study confirms that expectation-outcome discrepancies correlate with reduced satisfaction and decreased willingness to undergo surgery again. Addressing unrealistic expectations in the preoperative phase is recommended [ ]. Almost 80% would reconsider surgery, with satisfaction independent of weight loss or reoperation rate but significantly associated with weight stability and expectation-outcome congruence. This pattern aligns with long-term literature showing no association between satisfaction and absolute weight loss, underscoring the multifaceted nature of postoperative satisfaction [ , ]. Satisfaction predictors evolve over time: weight loss and perceived health dominate at six months to two years, body dissatisfaction at one year [ ], while our 19-year data identify weight stability as a critical long-term determinant. Several factors may explain high satisfaction despite variable adherence and suboptimal outcomes. First, satisfaction may reflect relative improvement from preoperative state rather than achievement of ideal outcomes—even patients with substantial weight regain may experience meaningful gains compared to their pre-surgical condition. Second, patients may reframe expectations over time, shifting from weight-loss goals toward broader quality-of-life improvements. Third, having exhausted conservative treatments, patients may view surgery as their best available option regardless of imperfect outcomes. Finally, non-weight benefits including sustained comorbidity improvements, enhanced physical functioning, or psychosocial gains may persist independent of weight outcomes. The weight stability finding suggests that ongoing fluctuations diminish satisfaction. This warrants replication. 4.7 Encountered barriers and peer advice Reported barriers encompassed eating and drinking, physical, psychological, and social domains. Some participants felt isolated and lonely due to inadequate understanding and support within their social networks, both regarding the initial decision to undergo surgery and during the long-term postoperative adaptation. This finding aligns with research indicating that social support is a critical factor in bariatric surgery outcomes, and highlights the importance of support systems into comprehensive bariatric care programs [ ]. To our knowledge, no previous study examined patient-reported barriers, though reported challenges overlapped with studies investigating unmet expectations [ ]. Barriers underrepresented in literature included dental issues [ ] and endocrinological complications such as pancreatitis and gallstones [ ], warranting broader examination of long-term consequences. Peer advice ranged from recommendation to cautionary guidance and emphasized gathering comprehensive information from multiple sources, characterizing surgery as a weight loss tool rather than comprehensive solution. Recommendations highlighted awareness of emotional eating's impact, dietary guideline adherence, sustained effort for maintaining results, and social support value. These patient recommendations align with our quantitative findings, highlighting three priority areas for long-term follow-up: sustained nutritional monitoring (given one-third minimal vitamin use), ongoing behavioral support for eating patterns (particularly snacking control), and weight stability monitoring with early intervention to prevent regain and dissatisfaction. However, our study was conducted before the advent of GLP-1 agonist therapy for post-bariatric weight management. Given the emerging role of these medications in managing weight regain after bariatric surgery, future studies should examine their use, effectiveness, and patient perspectives in long-term follow-up cohorts. Our findings align with our previously published 5-year study [ ], confirming persistent eating behavior challenges, vitamin non-adherence and satisfaction independent of absolute weight loss. Novel insights from the 19-year follow-up include: (1) weight stability—rather than absolute loss—as the key satisfaction predictor, (2) expectation-outcome congruence as critical for satisfaction, and (3) patient wisdom characterizing surgery as a 'tool requiring lifelong effort' rather than cure. 4.8 Limitations This study contributes to the limited body of long-term bariatric outcomes research, particularly from patient perspectives. Nevertheless, several limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, contemporary procedures (gastric sleeve, gastric bypass) differ from those undergone by participants. However, no evidence suggests modern procedures specifically impede or facilitate postoperative lifestyle adaptation. Additionally, LAGB management remains relevant in many bariatric practices [ ]. Postoperative guidelines remain largely unchanged, and long-term behavioral studies remain scarce. Therefore, these findings likely provide meaningful insights into long-term postoperative behaviors. Second, response rate was relatively low, a common challenge in long-term follow-up studies. These exploratory findings require replication in future research. Finally, self-report bias (overreporting positive outcomes, underreporting negative outcomes) cannot be excluded. However, current findings align with other long-term studies incorporating objective weight assessment. Moreover, this study prioritized patient perspectives to capture subjective experiences regarding benefits and risks, which makes self-report essential. 5 Conclusions Long-term adherence to healthy lifestyle behaviors and dietary guidelines was inconsistent. Most patients would reconsider bariatric surgery. Satisfaction did not depend on weight loss or reoperation, while weight instability and expectation-outcome discrepancies reduced surgical reconsideration likelihood. Defining success solely through weight loss outcomes and comorbidity reduction may inadequately represent patient perspectives. We advocate for lifelong follow-up to optimize postoperative results. documents.title: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in the Intensive Care Unit

chunks.content: Introduction Acute gastrointestinal injury (AGI) is a common and clinically significant complication among critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the intensive care unit (ICU) [ ]. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) first clearly defined AGI in 2012 as gastrointestinal dysfunction in critically ill patients caused by acute disease, characterized by impaired gastrointestinal motility, malabsorption, and intestinal barrier disruption, with severe cases potentially leading to intestinal ischemia or necrosis [ ]. Recent evidence indicates that the incidence of AGI in mechanically ventilated patients can reach up to 60% [ , ]. First, the impaired intestinal barrier integrity associated with AGI leads to bacterial translocation and endotoxin release, exacerbating the systemic inflammatory response [ ]. Second, AGI impairs nutrient absorption, leading to negative nitrogen balance and immunosuppression [ ]. Third, and most importantly, AGI is significantly associated with multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, increasing the risk of death two- to three-fold [ , ]. Additionally, AGI prolongs ICU hospitalization, increases medical costs, and leads to secondary complications such as malnutrition and infection, imposing a heavy burden on both patients and the healthcare system [ ]. Positive-pressure ventilation restricts diaphragmatic movement, increases intra-abdominal pressure, and reduces visceral blood flow, ultimately leading to mucosal hypoxia and gastrointestinal dysfunction [ , ]. Currently, diagnosis primarily relies on the ESICM AGI grading criteria. Although objective biomarkers are lacking, validation studies on candidate biomarkers such as D-lactate and diamine oxidase have made progress [ ], but their translational application remains limited. Existing risk factor analyses for AGI patients have primarily focused on single factors, with few comprehensive multi-factor analyses and limited research on the dynamic effects of pharmacological factors such as vasoactive medications. This study aims to identify factors associated with AGI through a retrospective analysis of routine clinical data from patients receiving IMV. Methods Study design and population This study was a retrospective, single-center, observational cohort study conducted in two general ICUs at the two campuses of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University. The hospital is a tertiary-level general hospital with 1,881 beds, including 41 ICU beds. Study data were derived from the electronic medical records of patients who received IMV in the ICU between January 2020 and August 2023. As this was a non-interventional, retrospective, observational study involving only the analysis of standard medical care data, the associated risks were extremely low. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Fujian Medical University Affiliated Second Hospital [Ethics Review Document No. (115) of 2023 Fuzhou Medical University Affiliated Second Hospital], and informed consent was waived. This study was reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines. During the study period, 1,631 patients were admitted to the ICU, of whom 425 received IMV and met the inclusion criteria for analysis. All the enrolled patients met the following inclusion criteria: (1) age ≥ 18 years, (2) ICU stay ≥ 48 h, and (3) MV via endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy. Patients were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: (1) invasive MV duration < 24 h, (2) pregnancy, (3) malignant tumors, (4) near-death condition, (5) primary gastrointestinal disease causing gastrointestinal dysfunction, and (6) history of gastrointestinal surgery. Patients were divided into an AGI occurrence group and a control group based on whether AGI had occurred during their ICU stay. The sample size was not pre-calculated; all patients meeting the inclusion criteria were included in the analysis to ensure data comprehensiveness. The patient selection process is shown in Fig. . Data collection Research data obtained from the electronic medical record database of the hospital’s Intensive Care Clinical Information System. Two trained master’s degree students in nursing independently completed the data collection. Any discrepancies were arbitrated by a senior nursing expert with 20 years of ICU work experience. The primary approach to addressing any missing core data was contacting the original attending physician or medical recorder for supplementation. All risk factor data in this study were collected before the onset of AGI to comply with the temporal sequence requirements of a retrospective study. This study focused on new-onset AGI developed during the ICU stay. The time to first occurrence of AGI was calculated from ICU admission to the first documented diagnosis of AGI that met the study criteria. The time to initiation of enteral nutrition(EN) was defined as the duration (in days) from ICU admission to the first administration of enteral nutrition in the ICU. Patients who were already receiving any form of enteral nutrition prior to ICU admission were excluded from this analysis. The collected data included: General information: age, sex, IMV method, EN method, history of diabetes, history of hypertension, history of previous abdominal surgery, underlying disease, Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score, and Nutritional Risk Screening (NRS) 2002 score. Laboratory test results: hemoglobin count, serum

of AGI that met the study criteria. The time to initiation of enteral nutrition(EN) was defined as the duration (in days) from ICU admission to the first administration of enteral nutrition in the ICU. Patients who were already receiving any form of enteral nutrition prior to ICU admission were excluded from this analysis. The collected data included: General information: age, sex, IMV method, EN method, history of diabetes, history of hypertension, history of previous abdominal surgery, underlying disease, Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score, and Nutritional Risk Screening (NRS) 2002 score. Laboratory test results: hemoglobin count, serum albumin count, and lymphocyte count. Clinical-related data: Time to first occurrence of AGI, time to initiation of EN, duration of IMV, administration of catecholamine drugs, administration of sedative/analgesic drugs, length of ICU stay, length of hospital stay, and duration of EN. AGI symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, gastric retention, hyperactive/hypoactive/absent bowel sounds, constipation, and abdominal distension. Statistical methods Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0 and R software (version 4.5.1). Continuous variables that followed a normal distribution were expressed as mean ± SD and compared using the Student’s t-test. Non-normally distributed data were expressed as the median with quartiles (Q1, Q3) and analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Measurement data were checked for normality, and the proportions were compared using the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. Binary logistic regression analysis was performed to screen for risk factors. After univariate analysis was performed to identify variables with a significance of P < 0.05, multivariate models including these variables were developed to identify independent risk factors (odds ratio [OR] > 1) and protective factors (OR < 1). Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank tests for group comparisons. The proportional hazards assumption was evaluated using Schoenfeld residuals, with standard Cox regression serving as the primary analytical method. Sensitivity analyses included time-dependent Cox models and restricted mean survival time analysis. Associations were expressed as hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Results Baseline characteristics of study participants This study evaluated 425 eligible patients of a median age of 60 years (IQR 48 to 70), of whom 290 (68.2%) were males. Their baseline characteristics are presented in Table . The incidence of AGI was 67.5%, The median time to first occurrence was 5 days (IQR 4 to 8) from ICU admission, with 73.2% of cases developing within the first week admission to the ICU. The most common gastrointestinal symptom among ICU patients receiving IMV was gastric retention (50.52%), followed by diarrhea (35.89%). MV was primarily administered via nasotracheal/endotracheal intubation (66.4%), with tracheostomy being more commonly used in the occurrence group (38.0% vs. 24.6%). Assessment of disease severity indicated that the APACHE II score ( P < 0.001) was significantly higher in the occurrence group than in the control group. The time to initiation of EN was similar between the two groups, EN was initiated within 48 h of ICU admission in 297 patients (69.9%) of the entire cohort. The two groups were similar in terms of age, sex, and underlying diseases. As shown in Table . Comparison of clinical data between the occurrence and control groups Multiple clinical indicators significantly differed between the two groups. Patients in the occurrence group had a significantly longer duration of IMV than those in the control group (median: 12 [IQR 5 to 17] vs. 6 [IQR 4 to 8] days, respectively, P < 0.001). The occurrence group had a significantly higher rate of sedation/analgesia drug administration (89.2% vs. 77.5%, respectively, P = 0.001). The duration of EN support was significantly longer for the patients in the occurrence group (median: 12 [IQR 7 to 17] vs. 7 [IQR 5 to 12.25] days, respectively, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the patients in the occurrence group were administered catecholamine drugs significantly more frequently (90.2% vs. 68.8%, respectively, P < 0.001). As shown in Table . Logistic regression analysis of AGI in ICU patients on IMV This study investigated the risk factors for AGI in ICU patients receiving IMV using univariate and multivariate logistic regression analysis. Univariate analysis revealed that the following factors were significantly associated with the occurrence of AGI (all P < 0.05): IMV method, elevated APACHE II score, elevated hemoglobin count, increased nutritional risk, prolonged IMV duration, administration of sedative/analgesic drugs, prolonged duration of EN, administration of catecholamine drugs, prolonged length of ICU stay, prolonged length of hospital stay, and underlying respiratory system disease. Multivariate analysis identified the following factors as independent associated with the occurrence of AGI: APACHE II score (adjusted OR [aOR]: 1.119, P < 0.001), NRS 2002 score (aOR: 1.416, P = 0.001), administration of catecholamine drugs (aOR: 2.881, P = 0.001), duration of IMV (aOR: 1.142, P < 0.001), and respiratory system disease (aOR: 2.097, P = 0.012), as shown in Table . Survival analysis of association

increased nutritional risk, prolonged IMV duration, administration of sedative/analgesic drugs, prolonged duration of EN, administration of catecholamine drugs, prolonged length of ICU stay, prolonged length of hospital stay, and underlying respiratory system disease. Multivariate analysis identified the following factors as independent associated with the occurrence of AGI: APACHE II score (adjusted OR [aOR]: 1.119, P < 0.001), NRS 2002 score (aOR: 1.416, P = 0.001), administration of catecholamine drugs (aOR: 2.881, P = 0.001), duration of IMV (aOR: 1.142, P < 0.001), and respiratory system disease (aOR: 2.097, P = 0.012), as shown in Table . Survival analysis of association between catecholamine drug administration and AGI risk in ICU patients Survival analysis revealed a significant association between catecholamine drug administration and AGI risk in ICU patients (log-rank χ² = 7.65, P = 0.0057). Schoenfeld residual test indicated that the proportional hazards assumption was not violated ( P = 0.288). Standard Cox proportional hazards regression confirmed this association (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.709, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.157 to 2.525, P = 0.007). Sensitivity analyses further supported the robustness of these findings. Time-dependent Cox regression showed no significant time-varying effect (interaction term P = 0.484), and restricted mean survival time analysis at 6 days demonstrated a significant between-group difference of -0.286 days ( P = 0.033). Additionally, piecewise Cox regression stratified at 6 days revealed consistently elevated AGI risk associated with catecholamine use in both the early (0–6 days: HR = 2.042, 95% CI: 1.302 to 3.202, P = 0.002) and late phases (> 6 days: HR = 2.798, 95% CI: 1.228 to 6.374, P = 0.014), suggesting a possible time-dependent increase in risk magnitude. The consistent results across multiple analytical approaches confirm the association between catecholamine drug administration and increased AGI risk, underscoring the importance of gastrointestinal function monitoring in ICU patients receiving these medications, as shown in Fig. . Discussion This study made three major findings that contribute to the literature. First, this study revealed identified factors independently associated with the occurrence of AGI. Second, it uncovered the dynamic association between catecholamine drug exposure time and AGI risk. Third, it demonstrated that catecholamine drugs, EN, and AGI may interact through multiple pathways to form a dynamic equilibrium. Numerous clinical studies have demonstrated that EN exerts a significant protective effect against AGI. A systematic review reported that the early initiation of EN could reduce the risk of AGI through several mechanisms [ ]. In one mechanism, the glutamine and short-chain fatty acids provided by EN, such as butyrate, significantly enhance the expression of the tight junction proteins occludin and ZO-1 in intestinal epithelial cells, thereby maintaining the integrity of the intestinal mucosal barrier [ ]. In another, EN increases mesenteric blood flow, significantly improving intestinal microcirculation [ ]. Additionally, EN maintains the balance of the commensal microbiota, reducing the overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria, thereby lowering endotoxin translocation and systemic inflammatory responses [ , ]. Further studies indicate that EN reduces the incidence of infection-related complications and gastrointestinal dysfunction [ ]. This study found no significant association between the timing of EN initiation, its duration, or the EN method and the occurrence of acute gastrointestinal injury (AGI). This result may stem from the combined effects of the following multi-layered factors: First, EN was initiated exceptionally early in our cohort, with 69.9% of patients starting EN within 48 h of ICU admission. This high degree of clinical consistency resulted in minimal differences between the “early” and “late” groups, an imbalance in sample size distribution, and a significant reduction in the statistical power to detect potential subtle effects of timing, a well-known limitation in studies with highly standardized practices. Particularly in shock states, the decision to initiate EN is governed more by achieving hemodynamic stability than by a fixed time window, as emphasized in recent guidelines which prioritize vasopressor dose and perfusion targets over a rigid 48-hour rule [ ]. Second, the standardized selection of EN methods: The majority of patients (60.5%) received feeding via a nasogastric tube, reflecting routine ICU practice based on safety and feasibility. Nasoenteric tubes may have been reserved for specific high-risk patients, leading to an imbalance in baseline risks among the different EN method groups and confounding their true association with AGI. Third, EN tolerance as a more critical mediating variable: Compared to “whether feeding is provided” or “how long it is administered,” “whether feeding is well tolerated” may be a more direct pathway linking EN to AGI. Recent prospective studies have identified for patients who have developed AGI, a cautious, stepwise approach to EN—transitioning from limited to progressive feeding as tolerance allows—is strongly recommended to avoid exacerbating intestinal injury [ ]. Intolerance manifestations such as high gastric residual volume and diarrhea following EN initiation are themselves clinical features or precursors of AGI. A recent meta-analysis highlights that

true association with AGI. Third, EN tolerance as a more critical mediating variable: Compared to “whether feeding is provided” or “how long it is administered,” “whether feeding is well tolerated” may be a more direct pathway linking EN to AGI. Recent prospective studies have identified for patients who have developed AGI, a cautious, stepwise approach to EN—transitioning from limited to progressive feeding as tolerance allows—is strongly recommended to avoid exacerbating intestinal injury [ ]. Intolerance manifestations such as high gastric residual volume and diarrhea following EN initiation are themselves clinical features or precursors of AGI. A recent meta-analysis highlights that this protective effect exhibits a clear dose-dependent relationship: In patients with AGI grade II or higher, full-dose EN increases the risk of feeding intolerance 2.1-fold, indicating the need to adjust EN strategies based on AGI grading [ ]. Catecholamine drugs are critical determinants of EN delivery. Research indicates that low to moderate doses of catecholamine drugs do not interfere with EN initiation, while higher doses may impair visceral blood flow and reduce EN tolerance [ ]. In a study where 93% of shock patients received catecholamine therapy at enrollment, a significantly higher incidence of gastrointestinal intolerance was observed in the EN group compared with the parenteral nutrition group [ ]. Gastrointestinal intolerance is associated with gastrointestinal motility disorders in shock states, and catecholamines or systemic inflammatory responses may further exacerbate these disorders [ ]. Other studies have confirmed that catecholamines are significantly negatively correlated with EN tolerance [ ]. The European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism guidelines explicitly recommend delaying the initiation of EN in patients with hemodynamic instability requiring high-dose catecholamines until hemodynamic stability is achieved [ ]. After shock is controlled and low-dose catecholamines are administered, therapeutic feeding may be initiated. Research indicates that administration of catecholamine drugs is is strongly associated with AGI. In a study by Merdji et al. catecholamine-induced microcirculatory dysfunction led to mucosal ischemia and barrier disruption, creating a vicious cycle: Microcirculatory failure exacerbated AGI, while the inflammatory response associated with AGI further damaged the microcirculation [ ]. Xue-Mei et al. confirmed this mechanism through biomarker studies, showing that the high-dose group had significantly elevated levels of intestinal fatty acid-binding protein, this association may stem from α1-adrenergic receptor-mediated visceral hypoperfusion, leading to intestinal ischemic injury and promoting the development of AGI [ ]. The use of EN, administration of catecholamine drugs, and AGI appear to be interconnected in a complex pathophysiological network. Although EN is thought to exert protective effects by maintaining intestinal barrier function and improving microcirculation, these potential benefits might be counteracted in the presence of high-dose catecholamine drugs through α1 receptor-mediated visceral hypoperfusion, which could potentially exacerbate AGI. Furthermore, prolonged use of catecholamines can further exacerbate intestinal microcirculatory dysfunction, forming a pathological positive feedback loop. Among the research, one study found that 92.13% of patients developed AGI within the first week of ICU admission [ ], while another study reported that 88.13% of patients developed AGI [ ].The incidence rate in this study is lower than that reported in the previous two studies. This may be related to the lower median age of the patients in this study and the exclusion of patients with primary gastrointestinal diseases and a history of gastrointestinal surgery. Older adults are more prone to AGI, and their declining gastrointestinal function can lead to the rapid onset of compensatory diseases [ ]. The results of this study show that AGI in these patients primarily manifests as gastric retention, diarrhea, and constipation, while another study reported vomiting, diarrhea, and gastroparesis as the main manifestations [ ]. These differences primarily stem from variations in conceptual definitions and population characteristics [ ]. Notably, diarrhea was a prominent symptom in both studies, and its high incidence may be associated with multiple factors, such as EN management, the use of prokinetic agents, and antibiotic-associated dysbiosis [ ]. Clinical management should incorporate individualized strategies based on underlying conditions, medication history, and dynamic monitoring results. This study revealed the pathophysiological mechanisms by which primary respiratory diseases, duration of IMV, and length of hospital stay all influence the occurrence of AGI. Patients with respiratory diseases often require longer IMV support due to hypoxemia and hypercapnia [ ]. Prolonged IMV inevitably prolongs hospitalization, leading to cumulative administration of sedative/analgesic drugs and broad-spectrum antibiotics, which directly inhibit gastrointestinal motility and disrupt intestinal microbiota balance [ ]. Furthermore, bed-related muscle weakness and increased intra-abdominal pressure further exacerbate gastrointestinal dysfunction [ ]. Therefore, healthcare providers should identify high-risk populations early in treatment and actively provide early rehabilitation activities to improve metabolic function and visceral nerve innervation across organs, thereby preventing or alleviating gastrointestinal dysfunction and mitigate the risk of its progression. Limitations First, the two-year interval since data collection may have seen continued evolution in clinical guidelines and

Prolonged IMV inevitably prolongs hospitalization, leading to cumulative administration of sedative/analgesic drugs and broad-spectrum antibiotics, which directly inhibit gastrointestinal motility and disrupt intestinal microbiota balance [ ]. Furthermore, bed-related muscle weakness and increased intra-abdominal pressure further exacerbate gastrointestinal dysfunction [ ]. Therefore, healthcare providers should identify high-risk populations early in treatment and actively provide early rehabilitation activities to improve metabolic function and visceral nerve innervation across organs, thereby preventing or alleviating gastrointestinal dysfunction and mitigate the risk of its progression. Limitations First, the two-year interval since data collection may have seen continued evolution in clinical guidelines and management strategies, which could affect the current applicability of our findings to some extent. Furthermore, the retrospective design is susceptible to common biases variability in AGI diagnostic criteria among different clinicians. Nonetheless, the results of this study provide valuable preliminary evidence in this field. Future research should employ larger-scale, multicenter, prospective designs to validate these findings and further promote the standardization of AGI diagnostic criteria and the optimization of intervention strategies. Conclusion The findings of this study indicate that the occurrence of AGI in ICU patients undergoing IMV is characterized by a early-stage incidence and is influenced by multiple factors. Based on the characteristics of the risk factors, the following clinical recommendations are proposed: (1) implementation of dynamic gastrointestinal function assessment in the early stages of IMV; (2) reduction of risk through combined interventions of individualized ventilation strategies and gastrointestinal protection early in treatment; and (3) establishment of a preventive management process for high-risk patients.

documents.title: ESPEN Practical Guideline Clinical Nutrition in Surgery

chunks.content: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This pilot randomised controlled trial will assess the feasibility and acceptability of an implementation strategy to improve nutrition care delivery in pancreatic cancer compared with implementation as usual. Key strengths include the use of an established protocol for nutrition counselling delivery and the use of patient-mediated tools, such as a question prompt list, to better engage patients in nutrition care delivery. Key limitations include a single-site study design and the inability to evaluate long-term changes in patient outcomes (beyond 6 months) due to the short timeframe of study. Introduction When pancreatic cancer is detected early, surgery can help individuals with pancreatic cancer live longer. While surgery improves patient outcomes, it can negatively affect patients’ nutritional status. Studies estimate that~60–80% of patients experience weight loss after pancreatic cancer surgery. Pancreatic surgical patients are at high risk of malnutrition for several reasons. Pancreatic surgery can lead to a loss in digestive enzyme production, making it difficult to absorb nutrients from food. Pancreatic surgery can cause a breakdown of the body’s energy and protein stores, causing weight loss and muscle breakdown. Patients may also experience nutrition-impact symptoms that affect the ability and desire to eat (eg, loss of appetite, feeling full early), which can be caused by the cancer and/or the surgery. Post-operative malnutrition is distressing for patients and caregivers and can negatively affect patients’ quality of life, surgical recovery and survival. Malnutrition can also affect healthcare systems through increased hospital length of stay, readmission and healthcare costs. To reduce malnutrition, clinical guidelines for pancreatic cancer recommend nutrition counselling from a dietitian, an evidence-based intervention for improving nutritional status. In practice, access and delivery of nutrition counselling after pancreatic cancer surgery varies across settings. Prior studies suggest that pancreatic cancer patients do not receive sufficient nutrition support after hospital discharge. Studies estimate that less than half of pancreatic cancer surgery patients meet with a dietitian after hospital discharge. Pancreatic cancer patients and their caregivers often report feeling overwhelmed and underprepared to manage nutrition once they transition from hospital to home. Post-operative nutritional status plays a pivotal role in patients’ surgical recovery, quality of life and survival. Therefore, improving access and delivery of nutrition counselling after hospital discharge is an important priority for cancer care delivery. To address this priority, there are barriers that hinder nutrition counselling delivery after surgery that need to be addressed. Most healthcare settings lack standardised protocols for referring patients to a dietitian after pancreatic cancer surgery. While there are protocols to ensure nutrition counselling is delivered during hospitalisation, there is limited guidance on when or how much nutrition counselling should be delivered once patients are discharged home. Similarly, few healthcare settings collect patient-reported information, such as nutrition-impact symptoms, that may be important for monitoring nutrition and tailoring nutrition counselling post-discharge. For example, dietitians may not be aware a patient is experiencing steatorrhoea—an important indicator of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency—unless a patient reports this information. Patient-reported information can prompt patients to report nutrition-impact symptoms. There are also barriers that affect patient engagement in nutrition counselling. Patients may lack an understanding of how a dietitian can support their cancer care journey or the potential value of nutrition counselling; as a consequence, patients may decline to meet with a dietitian when referred. Patients may lack the resources or skills needed to participate in and adhere to nutrition counselling recommendations (eg, tracking dietary goals, food security). To overcome these barriers, strategies are needed to standardise post-surgical nutrition counselling, collect patient-reported information and provide patient-mediated strategies to support pancreatic cancer patient engagement in nutrition counselling. In response to this challenge, our study team developed the Support through Remote Observation and Nutrition Guidance (STRONG) programme, which includes three components: (1) a standardised protocol for nutrition counselling after hospital discharge, (2) exchange of patient-reported information between dietitians and patients and (3) nutrition management tools (question prompt list, educational brochure). The proposed study will outline a pilot randomised controlled trial of the STRONG programme in pancreatic cancer surgery patients after hospital discharge. The trial will compare the STRONG programme with usual care (nutrition care implementation as usual) using a pragmatic design with broad inclusion criteria and integration within existing care teams and workflows. The study’s primary aim is to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the STRONG programme among patients, caregivers and healthcare providers. The study’s secondary aim is to collect preliminary data on implementation and effectiveness outcomes that may be associated with the STRONG programme. The long-term goal of this research is to improve nutrition care access and delivery among pancreatic cancer patients who are transitioning from hospital to home after surgery, which has the potential to improve patient, caregiver and healthcare system outcomes. Study findings will be used to refine the STRONG implementation strategy and inform a future definitive hybrid

The long-term goal of this research is to improve nutrition care access and delivery among pancreatic cancer patients who are transitioning from hospital to home after surgery, which has the potential to improve patient, caregiver and healthcare system outcomes. Study findings will be used to refine the STRONG implementation strategy and inform a future definitive hybrid implementation-effectiveness trial. Methods and analysis Study design and setting The proposed pilot study will use a parallel randomised controlled trial design and be implemented at a single site, Moffitt Cancer Center (Moffitt), a standalone National Cancer Institute-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida. Participants will be randomised 1:1 to the STRONG programme or usual care. Given the pragmatic nature of the trial, and the goal to inform real-world care delivery, the comparator selected is usual care. The intervention will last for the post-surgical recovery period, 8 weeks, and participants will complete study assessments at baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks (end of intervention) and 12 weeks (see Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) 2025 participant timeline in ). Exit interviews will be conducted with a subset of participants and caregivers and oncology providers (eg, dietitians, nurses, surgeons) who support STRONG implementation. This protocol has been reported in accordance with SPIRIT 2025 reporting guidelines. Participants will receive a US$25 gift card for each study assessment completed (up to four study assessments or US$100 in gift cards). Individuals completing the exit interview will receive a US$50 gift card for interview completion. The study is planned to last 4 years from August 2023 to August 2027. Development of a Theoretical Domains Framework-informed patient-mediated strategy The Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) identifies psychological, social and environmental influences that affect behaviour change among healthcare providers and patients. The study team used the TDF to identify and prioritise target behaviours and barriers to clinician and patient behaviour change based on a literature review and qualitative research. The prioritised barriers included (1) lack of standardised protocols for nutrition counselling post-discharge, (2) lack of patient-reported nutrition information to monitor nutrition and tailor nutrition counselling, (3) lack of patient awareness and perceived value of nutrition counselling; and (4) lack of patient resources and skills needed to participate in and adhere to nutrition counselling recommendations. TDF-informed barriers were mapped to the COM-B model, which stands for Capability (C), Opportunity (O), Motivation (M) and Behaviour (B), and linked to the behaviour change wheel, which informed the selection of the behaviour change techniques guiding each strategy. The STRONG implementation logic model is displayed in . STRONG includes systems-level change including an electronic health record (EHR) order for a standardised nutrition protocol that includes an initial nutrition counselling session within 1 week of hospital discharge and bi-weekly follow-up for 8 weeks after surgery (four total sessions). The timing and amount of counselling was based on feedback from clinicians, caregivers and patients. We wanted to ensure early, intensive and ongoing nutrition support after hospital discharge, which is encouraged in clinical guidelines for pancreatic surgery. The aim of the standardised protocol is to reduce complexity and allow healthcare providers to place a one-time EHR order set for a bundle of nutrition counselling visits rather than ad-hoc scheduling of nutrition counselling visits. Prior studies suggest that standardised EHR order sets can improve evidence-based care delivery. Research suggests that referring patients for nutrition counselling and other services (eg, supportive care) may not be sufficient to ensure patient uptake. Prior studies have shown that education about the goal of the visit and its potential value prior to the visit may increase cancer patient uptake of nutrition counselling and similar services. To address this, the study team developed a question prompt list that reviews the benefits of nutrition counselling and provides a list of questions that other pancreatic cancer surgery patients have found helpful to ask the dietitian after hospital discharge. Prior studies have demonstrated that question prompt lists can be effective for improving patient activation, communication self-efficacy and engagement in clinic visits. Patients will also be provided with tools to support nutrition self-management, including an educational booklet about common eating problems after pancreatic surgery and potential dietary strategies and an electronic or paper food diary to track food intake and nutrition-impact symptoms and share patient-reported information with the dietitian. Prior research demonstrates that dietitians may not have sufficient patient-reported information to monitor malnutrition and tailor nutrition counselling visits and that collection of patient-reported information may be a feasible strategy for addressing this barrier. To build on this research, STRONG collects patient-reported information from two sources: (1) food diary

engagement in clinic visits. Prior research demonstrates that dietitians may not have sufficient patient-reported information to monitor malnutrition and tailor nutrition counselling visits and that collection of patient-reported information may be a feasible strategy for addressing this barrier. To build on this research, STRONG collects patient-reported information from two sources: (1) food diary that patients complete between visits that tracks food intake and nutrition symptoms, (2) study assessments that assess nutritional status via Patient-Generated Subjective Global Assessment (PG-SGA) short-form and (3) an EHR documentation template with a script that prompts dietitians to collect information on food preferences (eg, cultural or religious preferences), food insecurity and other nutrition barriers (eg, ability to prepare food) that may affect nutrition counselling delivery. The patient-reported information is accessible in a web-based dashboard. The patient-reported information is intended to help dietitians focus the visit on patients’ needs and preferences (eg, provide dietary recommendations that consider affordability concerns). Previous research in oncology has shown that patient-reported information can improve the delivery of patient-centred and individualised care. The long-term goal of this line of research is to improve nutrition care delivery for pancreatic cancer surgery patients after hospital discharge, a time when patients report feeling overwhelmed and underprepared to manage nutrition. The proposed study aims to improve nutrition counselling access and delivery, which is hypothesised to improve service delivery outcomes (eg, timeliness and patient-centredness of nutrition care, hospital readmissions) and patient outcomes (eg, nutritional status, quality of life and survival) ( ). Participant eligibility Participants who meet the following criteria will be eligible: (1) ≥ 18 years of age; (2) diagnosis of pancreatic cancer; (3) completed pancreatic surgery (eg, Whipple procedure, distal/subtotal pancreatectomy, total pancreatectomy) at Moffitt; (4) able to provide informed consent in Spanish or English; and (5) discharged home on an oral diet. Participants will be excluded if they are determined to be ineligible for surgery during evaluation (eg, cancer metastasis). Recruitment and consent Study staff will be trained in human subjects, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the study protocol (eg, participate in mock consent) prior to participant enrolment. Study staff will communicate with inpatient clinic staff to identify potentially eligible patients and determine an appropriate time to approach patients (eg, after the patient has been advanced to a diet of clear liquids). Study staff will screen the EHR for the minimum information necessary to identify potentially eligible patients. Study staff will approach patients in person or call or videoconference patients who cannot be reached in person. Study staff will provide an overview of the study and assess interest. Among patients who were interested, study staff will review key elements of informed consent and obtain written informed consent ( ). The informed consent will contain subject injury language. The study team will request a waiver of HIPAA authorisation for EHR screening and to retain minimal information on participants who decline to participate (eg, sex, race/ethnicity, age, language preference, reason for decline), data that will be important for evaluating potential disparities in STRONG implementation. Randomisation A study team member with guidance from the study statistician will develop a randomisation table using Stata (StataCorp. 2025; College Station, TX: StataCorp LC.) that will be integrated into REDCap. Randomisation will include allocating 80 participants 1:1 to the STRONG programme vs usual care and will be stratified based on surgical procedure (eg, Whipple, total pancreatectomy or partial/sub-total distal pancreatectomy) given that each procedure can affect nutrition differently. To maintain balance across groups and concealment, block randomisation (in variable block sizes of four and six) will be used. The study statistician and outcome assessors will be blinded to group allocation. Intervention condition Before hospital discharge, patients who are randomised to STRONG will meet with a study coordinator to go over study materials. The materials include a question prompt list, an educational brochure that covers common eating problems after pancreatic surgery and recommended dietary strategies, and tips for keeping a food diary (eg, how to estimate portion size). Caregivers will be included in training when available. The study coordinator will assess the participants’ preferences for recording nutrition-impact symptoms and food intake and provide participants with a choice of an electronic option (eg, text message survey and food logging through Fitbit Inspire 3.0) or a paper option (paper food and symptom diary). The study coordinator will review with the participant and caregiver (when available) how to use the electronic or paper method. The study coordinator will use the teach-back method to confirm the participant understands how to use the tools. While the
