The study coordinator will review with the participant and caregiver (when available) how to use the electronic or paper method. The study coordinator will use the teach-back method to confirm the participant understands how to use the tools. While the participant is in the hospital, they will receive standard of care nutrition interventions including nutrition counselling from an inpatient dietitian. The study coordinator will contact the clinic team to make them aware the participant has enrolled. A designated member of the clinic team (eg, physician, advanced practice provider (APP)) will place an EHR order for the standardised nutrition protocol. The order includes an initial dietitian visit within 1 week of hospital discharge and bi-weekly follow-up visits for 8 weeks. The first nutrition counselling appointment will be an hour in length and can be completed remotely (videoconference, phone) or in person based on patient preference. Visit content is outlined in . Visit content is based on recommendations from oncology nutrition guidelines, a literature review and feedback from dietitians, patients and caregivers. Key content areas include a detailed nutrition assessment, screening for social needs (eg, food insecurity), discussion of food preferences, clarifying patient goals for nutrition and motivation for behaviour change, estimating energy requirements and providing tailored education and counselling. The visit content is similar to standard of care but is expanded to include a formal food insecurity screening through the Hunger Vital Sign tool, a validated assessment of nutritional status through the PG-SGA short-form, and review of patient-reported symptoms for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. The dietitian is encouraged to remind the participant at the end of the session about what is required between sessions (eg, using food diary) and timing of next session. Energy and protein requirement estimation will be based on European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) guidelines for clinical nutrition in cancer and may be modified based on dietitian judgement (eg, patient activity level, pre-existing malnutrition). After the first nutrition counselling appointment, the patient will meet with the dietitian on a bi-weekly basis during 30 min follow-up visits, with the exact timing determined based on patient and dietitian availability. Between visits, participants will be encouraged to log food intake and symptoms at least 3× a week (non-consecutive days) and complete a validated malnutrition screening tool once a month (PG-SGA short form). Prior studies suggest dietary assessment of 3 days of non-consecutive food records is sufficient for accurately estimating food intake while minimising participant burden (compared with daily food records). Dietitians will be given access to a dashboard that displays patient-reported information (eg, food intake and symptoms, nutritional status). Nutrition counselling sessions will be documented in the EHR, using a template that covers the key content of the visit (eg, results from food insecurity screening). The intervention will last for 8 weeks, a timeframe when nutritional impact symptoms are most severe and is often defined as the post-operative recovery window. Usual care condition Participants who are randomised to the usual care condition will receive the usual implementation of nutrition counselling. Clinic staff will refer patients to a dietitian when deemed necessary and patients will be provided with education about managing nutrition postoperatively. In usual care, prior studies have estimated that one out of four patients is referred to a dietitian after hospital discharge for pancreatic surgery in the US. As part of the proposed pilot study, we will document how much nutrition counselling and nutrition intervention is received by participants assigned to the usual care condition. The content of the nutritional counselling visits in usual care and how the content differs from the intervention group is outlined in . To ensure participants in the intervention and usual care condition receive similar educational content, participants in the usual care condition will receive the same educational brochure that the intervention group receives. Retention We will use the following strategies to maximise retention: (1) involve caregivers in STRONG training when feasible; (2) train participants and use the teach-back method to confirm understanding; (3) follow-up with participants after hospital discharge to check on the participant and see if they need any additional support or resources; (4) send reminders via email or text (when participant opts in for texting); (5) check in on participants who are not adhering to the programme; and (6) provide summaries that make participants aware of their progress (eg, 75% of study assessments are completed). Measures Study assessment schedule Participants will receive study assessments at baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks

retention: (1) involve caregivers in STRONG training when feasible; (2) train participants and use the teach-back method to confirm understanding; (3) follow-up with participants after hospital discharge to check on the participant and see if they need any additional support or resources; (4) send reminders via email or text (when participant opts in for texting); (5) check in on participants who are not adhering to the programme; and (6) provide summaries that make participants aware of their progress (eg, 75% of study assessments are completed). Measures Study assessment schedule Participants will receive study assessments at baseline, 4 weeks, 8 weeks (end of intervention) and 12 weeks. Data will also be collected through a food diary (app or paper log) and from the EHR at the end of the study. At 8 weeks, a subset of participants (n = 20) will have the option to participate in a one-time exit interview to provide feedback on the nutrition counselling and the patient-mediated implementation strategies (eg, patient-reported information collection, education, question prompt list). Participants in both the intervention and control group will be interviewed; the interview guide for control participants will focus on nutrition counselling received as a part of usual care (receipt, timing, quality) and not include questions about the STRONG programme. The study team will also conduct exit interviews with caregivers and clinicians (eg, dietitians, physicians, nurses) who participated in or supported STRONG implementation. Study assessments and intervention materials have already been translated and are available in Spanish and English. Primary outcomes The primary outcomes for the pilot randomised controlled trial are feasibility and acceptability. Feasibility will be measured by (1) recruitment rate; (2) data collection feasibility and (3) retention rate. We will document reasons for declining to participate and self-reported participant burden. We will document caregiver participation in the intervention through a survey question that assesses whether the patients’ caregiver provided support and what kind of support was provided (eg, assistance with food logging, preparing meals, attending visits) and explore caregiver participation in more detail through exit interviews (described below). Acceptability will be measured by satisfaction with the overall STRONG programme. For participants who opt to use the electronic food log, we will measure perceptions about the ease of use of the mobile application (usability). Data will be collected from screening logs, administrative data from the study database and the study assessments. Feasibility and acceptability outcomes observed in the pilot study will be compared with pre-planned benchmarks, which were developed based on similar studies. provides definitions for each measure and outlines pre-planned benchmarks. Secondary effectiveness outcomes The study will also collect preliminary data on patient and service delivery outcomes that may be impacted by STRONG. In a future definitive hybrid implementation effectiveness trial, nutritional status will serve as a primary endpoint and be measured using the PG-SGA short-form, a validated and widely used tool for identifying malnutrition in oncology. We will examine whether there is a clinically meaningful change in score (four points) and examine whether there are changes in the proportion of patients who are categorised as malnourished based on cut-offs established in prior research. Other indicators of malnutrition will be measured, including significant weight loss (defined as >5% and >10% of body weight), low body mass index (defined as <20 kg/m² for individuals <70 years old and <22 kg/m² for individuals ≥70 years old) and low skeletal muscle mass (ie, sarcopenia). Low muscle mass will be estimated by calculating skeletal muscle index (SMI) from routinely collected CT scans and defined as SMI ≤38.9 cm 2 /m 2 for females and SMI ≤55.4 cm 2 /m 2 for males, which is based on established cut-offs. Quality of life will be measured using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy General (FACT-G) scale. We will collect additional quality of life data, including the Functional Assessment of Anorexia/Cachexia Therapy subscale and the FACT–hepatobiliary scale. We will use minimal clinically important differences to evaluate change in quality of life score when available. Service delivery outcomes will include hospital readmissions (unplanned return to the hospital) within 30 and 90 days of hospital discharge. For readmissions outside of the index hospital, we will attempt to obtain a medical record release form to obtain relevant details (eg, reason for admission, date of admission). Exploratory outcomes In addition to our primary and secondary outcomes, we will collect exploratory data on the following outcomes. We will collect exploratory data on survival, which will be measured based on overall survival (time from random assignment to death from any cause) and progression-free survival (time from random assignment to disease progression or death from any cause). We will also measure the timeliness of nutrition counselling delivery (eg, median time from hospital discharge to first nutrition counselling visit) and patient perceptions about the patient-centredness of nutrition care using the Patient-Centred Communication in

(eg, reason for admission, date of admission). Exploratory outcomes In addition to our primary and secondary outcomes, we will collect exploratory data on the following outcomes. We will collect exploratory data on survival, which will be measured based on overall survival (time from random assignment to death from any cause) and progression-free survival (time from random assignment to disease progression or death from any cause). We will also measure the timeliness of nutrition counselling delivery (eg, median time from hospital discharge to first nutrition counselling visit) and patient perceptions about the patient-centredness of nutrition care using the Patient-Centred Communication in Cancer Care Short Form (6-item). We will collect exploratory data on implementation outcomes that may be associated with the STRONG programme based on the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) framework. In a future definitive hybrid implementation-effectiveness trial, the primary implementation outcome will be reach (proportion of target population that receives nutrition counselling within 1 week of hospital discharge). Other implementation outcomes to be collected include adoption (proportion of providers who referred patients to the study), implementation (fidelity, contamination, adaptation) and maintenance (impact of the intervention at 12 weeks). Fidelity will be measured based on how much intervention was delivered (eg, length of dietitian visits) and the proportion of key elements of nutrition counselling that were delivered (eg, individualised energy and protein requirements, screening for food insecurity). We will assess potential contamination, including use of patient-mediated strategies in the usual care group. Unplanned intervention or implementation strategy adaptations will be captured through periodic reflections with study and clinic staff and documented using the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications-Expanded (FRAME) methodology. Qualitative feedback A subset of participants (n = 20) will be invited to participate in a one-time, semi-structured interview at the end of the intervention. We will aim to have equal representation from intervention and control participants. The interview guide will ask participants to provide feedback on nutrition counselling (eg, receipt, timing, amount, quality, recommendations for improvement). The interview guide for the intervention group will include questions about the STRONG programme (eg, question prompt list, patient-reported information) and any barriers/facilitators to intervention uptake and/or strategy implementation. The guide will be based on the TDF. Individuals who participated in or supported implementation (eg, caregivers, healthcare providers) (n =10) will be asked to provide feedback about STRONG and barriers and facilitators to implementation. The interviews will be conducted via videoconference or phone, led by a staff member trained in qualitative methods, recorded and transcribed. We anticipate the interviews will last around 45 min. Exploratory mechanisms of change We will collect exploratory data on factors that may mediate the relationship between the STRONG implementation strategy and improved nutrition counselling implementation. The mechanisms of change that will be measured include patient activation (Patient Activation Measure 13-item) and patient self-efficacy for communicating with dietitians (Perceived Self-Efficacy Scale). Participant and treatment characteristics We will collect information on participant characteristics to describe the sample and characterise factors that may affect intervention or implementation effectiveness including demographics (eg, sex, age, race/ethnicity, language preference, digital and health literacy), clinical characteristics (eg, comorbidities) and treatment characteristics (eg, type of surgery, receipt of nutritional interventions). Data analyses Overall approach The primary goal of this pilot trial is to establish the feasibility of the STRONG programme and study procedures, and the secondary goal is to explore preliminary effects of STRONG on implementation, patient and service delivery outcomes. For preliminary effectiveness analyses, we will use an intent-to-treat approach to examine real-world effectiveness and conduct exploratory per-protocol analysis to explore effects in participants who adhered to the programme. We will evaluate the amount and pattern of missing data and potential sources of bias and adjust the statistical approach as needed. Plans for each Aim are described below. Aim 1 analyses Descriptive statistics will be used to summarise feasibility and acceptability outcomes and to compare outcomes against pre-planned benchmarks. Hybrid thematic analysis will be used to analyse interview transcripts. A codebook will be developed that includes deductive codes based on the interview guide, which is informed by the TDF. Inductive codes will also be developed based on themes that emerge from the data. Transcripts will be coded by two individuals who will come to a consensus regarding coding. The coders will use debriefs to discuss coding and interpretation and use analytic memos to document reflections. The study team will triangulate qualitative data with the quantitative data to look for data convergence. Data on feasibility, acceptability and other implementation outcomes will be used to refine the STRONG programme prior to a definitive trial. Aim 2 analyses Preliminary outcomes on effectiveness and implementation will be summarised and compared across conditions when appropriate (eg, proportion of participants in intervention vs control group that received nutrition counselling). Changes in patient outcomes will be measured over time (baseline,

to a consensus regarding coding. The coders will use debriefs to discuss coding and interpretation and use analytic memos to document reflections. The study team will triangulate qualitative data with the quantitative data to look for data convergence. Data on feasibility, acceptability and other implementation outcomes will be used to refine the STRONG programme prior to a definitive trial. Aim 2 analyses Preliminary outcomes on effectiveness and implementation will be summarised and compared across conditions when appropriate (eg, proportion of participants in intervention vs control group that received nutrition counselling). Changes in patient outcomes will be measured over time (baseline, 4, 8, 12 weeks) for two groups (intervention and control). To estimate changes in outcomes (eg, nutritional status) between groups, we will use linear mixed-effects models. Linear mixed-effects models account for dependence of longitudinal assessments and allow for participants with complete data to be included. Models will include fixed effects for time, group and group × time interaction, which measures differential change by group assignment. Models will adjust for randomisation strata and any group differences not balanced through randomisation. Mean differences will be compared against the threshold for a clinically significant difference (eg, 4-point change in PG-SGA score). Generalised estimating equations will be used to estimate change in binary outcomes (eg, presence/absence of severe malnutrition, readmissions). A Cox proportional hazards model will be used to analyse time to-event outcomes (eg, survival) and the model will be adjusted for randomisation strata and factors not balanced across groups. Model assumptions will be tested and the statistical approach will be adjusted as needed. Sample size considerations For this pilot study, the target enrolment is 80 participants. We assume that 15% will be lost due to attrition based on experience in our prior studies, leaving 68 or 34 participants per arm after attrition. We conducted a single-arm pilot study in this population and had a 15% attrition rate, which was used to estimate the attrition rate for this pilot study. Pilot clinical trial guidance suggests 25–35 participants per arm is sufficient to estimate feasibility and acceptability outcomes, such as recruitment and retention, and establish feasibility of study procedures. Data monitoring and interim analysis The principal investigator (PI) and study staff will meet weekly to review recruitment and retention, intervention adherence, adherence to study procedures, observed harms and data completion. The entire study team will meet monthly to discuss any protocol deviations or study implementation issues (eg, technical challenges with mobile app). Interim analysis for other study outcomes (eg, accrual of minority participants, participant acceptability and burden) will be evaluated on a quarterly basis. If feasibility and acceptability benchmarks are not achieved during interim analysis, or concerns are noted (eg, protocol deviation), we will review study procedures and consider pausing the study and/or modifying the study protocol until necessary changes have been implemented. This study has minimal risk and will not require external safety review. We do not anticipate any adverse events related to this minimal risk study. The main unanticipated problems that could occur are potential breaches of confidentiality, psychological distress and burden-related issues, which will be monitored. Study assessments will include participant self-report prompts to capture potential distress or burden related to the study protocol and staff will be provided with an adverse event log to note any observed distress, burden or confidentiality concerns. Institutional policies will be followed to report serious or unanticipated adverse events and the study will be paused until risk is assessed. Data security To protect participant data, we will use the following procedures. We will use participant identifiers to minimise the use of protected health information (PHI) on study forms and databases. We will limit the sharing of PHI to the minimum amount that is necessary and use encrypted methods for sharing PHI (eg, exchanging messages about participants for recruitment via EHR message when possible or encrypted email). Electronic data will be stored on a secure drive with access limited to study team members who need access (eg, research coordinator) and only accessible through an encrypted computer. Any PHI collected in paper form (eg, paper consent form for participants who cannot electronically sign) will be stored in a locked cabinet in a locked office. Paper PHI will be scanned, stored electronically on a secure drive and disposed of in a bin designated for shredding PHI. Audiovisual recordings will be collected through Zoom videoconference during exit interviews. Interviewers will be encouraged to have participants turn off their camera and to use participant identifiers instead of names so that PHI is not recorded. Recordings will be stored on a secure drive with limited access. Identifying data will be retained for 3 years following the conclusion of the study and then all identifying data will be securely deleted using approved methods. Design considerations To accommodate patient preferences, we opted to provide

scanned, stored electronically on a secure drive and disposed of in a bin designated for shredding PHI. Audiovisual recordings will be collected through Zoom videoconference during exit interviews. Interviewers will be encouraged to have participants turn off their camera and to use participant identifiers instead of names so that PHI is not recorded. Recordings will be stored on a secure drive with limited access. Identifying data will be retained for 3 years following the conclusion of the study and then all identifying data will be securely deleted using approved methods. Design considerations To accommodate patient preferences, we opted to provide patients with two options for logging food intake and symptoms, an electronic and paper option. We chose to include all types of pancreatic resections (eg, Whipple, total and distal pancreatectomy) given that malnutrition risk is high for all pancreatic surgery patients. Since some procedures carry a higher risk for malnutrition (eg, total vs distal pancreatectomy), we chose to stratify randomisation based on surgical procedure. Limitations This pilot trial will have several limitations, including a single-site study design and the ability to measure patient outcomes beyond 6 months due to the short timeframe of the study. The study is also not designed to collect information on cost, information important for future intervention planning. In a future definitive trial, we aim to collect information on intervention cost and cost-effectiveness. Ethics and dissemination The study protocol was approved by the Moffitt IRB of Record, Advarra (Pro00071143). The trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT06001268 ) prior to participant enrolment. The pilot trial is funded by the Department of Defense (DoD). The study team will share required study updates and findings through ClinicalTrials.gov. A plain language summary of study findings will be developed and shared back with participants, implementers and implementation supporters. Study findings will also be disseminated through conference abstracts and peer-reviewed publications. De-identified data supporting study findings will be deposited in the University of North Carolina (UNC) Dataverse repository at the conclusion of the study. Positive findings from the pilot study will be used to support STRONG refinement and planning of a definitive hybrid implementation-effectiveness trial. Patient and clinician involvement Development of this intervention involved extensive qualitative data collection and iterative testing from patients, caregivers and clinicians through methods such as in-depth interviews, cognitive interviews, co-design workshops and pilot testing, which will be reported elsewhere. Discussion Pilot studies are a critically important part of implementation research and help study teams to refine implementation procedures and ensure feasibility prior to conducting a larger definitive trial. This pilot study will test the feasibility and acceptability of STRONG, a patient-mediated implementation strategy to improve nutrition counselling delivery for pancreatic cancer surgical patients. There has been limited implementation research on overcoming common barriers to nutrition care delivery in oncology and limited research on engaging patients to improve the delivery of evidence-based care. Findings from this research could improve nutrition care delivery in oncology and patient, caregiver and healthcare system outcomes. Introduction Chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains a strong cause of adverse health outcomes, with a constant rise in prevalence and a recorded 41.5% global increase from 1990 to 2017 in all age-mortality rates [ ]. It was estimated that in 2017, 697.5 million people were diagnosed with any stage of CKD, which is equivalent to a 9.1% prevalence worldwide [ ]. Furthermore, it is expected that the number of patients receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) will be doubled by 2030, with the highest increase predicted for Asia and North America. This will eventually lead to a higher total cost of treatment, especially for patients with comorbidities, resulting in an economic burden on healthcare systems [ , ]. In order to avoid such a trend and avert an additional financial pressure on health systems, the development of low-cost strategies towards the prevention and reduction in the adverse outcomes of CKD is essential, if not critical [ ]. It has been well established that lifestyle and dietary modifications are a cost-effective strategy, producing both cost- and health-related benefits [ , , ]. In addition, improved nutritional status and compliance with the medical nutrition guidance has been positively associated with a better quality of life (QoL) and cognitive function, lower risk of complications (e.g., hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, cardiovascular, the progression of CKD, etc.), reduced risk of malnutrition and overall CKD-related symptoms [ , , ]. Therefore, it is essential for health professionals to comprehend the importance and complexity of the provision of nutritional support in these patients and emphasize the formulation and delivery of appropriate nutritional treatment followed by regular monitoring [ , ]. Such actions require the systematic development of clinical guidelines in order to ensure patients’ safety and provision of high-quality nutritional care [ ]. Clinical practice guidelines can be defined as evidence-based statements and recommendations aiming to enhance health outcomes of patients and simultaneously assist health professionals in their decision-making processes and implementation of individualized patient care [ ]. So far, a number of clinical guidelines have been published by several scientific societies, as well as international institutions and organizations, aiming to ensure the best nutritional management for patients with CKD. However, clinical practice guidelines often present high heterogeneity and a number of questions over their validity, reliability, applicability in clinical practice, transparency, and methodological rigor have been raised. In addition, there has not been any attempt to assess the quality and the development process of nutritional practice guidelines for patients with CKD. The aim of this study is to critically appraise the quality of existing clinical practice guidelines on the nutritional management of CKD and to identify their limitations and discrepancies with regard to structure, methodology, and development. Moreover, the provision of suggestions for potential areas of quality improvement is another scope of the present work, using the revised Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation tool (AGREE II), an international tool that has been widely used in the past 10 years for the quality assessment of medical guidelines, as the appraisal instrument [ ]. 2. Materials and Methods Systematic searches on PubMed, Scopus and Google scholar databases were performed (until 12th of November 2020) using the follow search string (guidelines OR recommendations OR statements) AND (CKD OR renal failure OR chronic kidney disease OR kidney failure) AND (nutrition OR diet OR nutritional management) for the PubMed database; this was modified accordingly for the other databases (see ). From a total 5687 results and after removing duplicates and irrelevant studies, 297 studies were screened for eligibility. Inclusion criteria were recently published nutritional guidelines for patients with CKD, developed by scientific societies and/or associations. Irrelevant recommendations, hospital internal guidelines or recommendations referring only to subjects <18 years old were excluded. Finally, 11 clinical practice guidelines published from 2003 until 2020 were retrieved [ , , , , , , , , , , ]. Clinical practice guidelines by the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral nutrition (ASPEN) [ ], the Dietitians Association of Australia (DAA) [ ], the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM) [ ], the European Best Practice Guidelines (EBPG) [ ], the European Dialysis and Transplantation Nurses Association-European Renal Care Association (EDTNA-ERCA) [ ], the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) [ , ], the Andalusian Group for Nutrition Reflection and Investigation (GARIN) group [ ], the National Kidney foundation-Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) [ ], the Italian Society of Nephrology-Association of Dieticians-Italian Association of Hemodialysis, Dialysis and Transplant (SIN-ANDID-ANED) [ ], and the Renal Association [ ] were reviewed and evaluated using the AGREE II tool. [ ] Translations of original clinical practice guidelines were excluded. The latest updated version of each guideline was selected for guidelines with previous published versions. Characteristics of eligible clinical practice guidelines that were included can be

Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) [ , ], the Andalusian Group for Nutrition Reflection and Investigation (GARIN) group [ ], the National Kidney foundation-Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) [ ], the Italian Society of Nephrology-Association of Dieticians-Italian Association of Hemodialysis, Dialysis and Transplant (SIN-ANDID-ANED) [ ], and the Renal Association [ ] were reviewed and evaluated using the AGREE II tool. [ ] Translations of original clinical practice guidelines were excluded. The latest updated version of each guideline was selected for guidelines with previous published versions. Characteristics of eligible clinical practice guidelines that were included can be found in . Guideline Appraisal Four authors, including medical doctors, nutritionists, and dietitians (DB, LC, KAP and MC), independently evaluated and appraised the 11 practice guidelines with the use of the AGREE II tool [ ]. Each reviewer ratings can be found in . The AGREE tool was first developed in 2003 in an effort to provide researchers with an instrument that would aid in the quality assessment, reporting, evaluation, and improvement of clinical practice guidelines within various health settings [ ]. The AGREE II tool, which is the updated version, consists of a reporting checklist including 23 items categorized under the following six main quality domains: 1. scope and purpose, 2. stakeholder involvement, 3. rigor of development, 4. clarity of presentation, 5. Applicability, and 6. editorial independence, as well as two more items under “overall assessment” concerning the overall quality of the guideline and recommendations on whether or not it should be used in practice [ ]. Each item is rated using a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Finally, the total score for each domain is calculated by summing up all ratings for all items of each domain and then expressed as a percentage of the maximum possible score in each domain, minus the minimum possible score as follows: (1) O b t a i n e d s c o r e − M i n i m u n p o s s i b l e s c o r e M a x i m u m p o s s i b l e s c o r e − M i n i m u m p o s s i b l e s c o r e × 100 In order to ensure the consistency regarding the evaluation of the included guidelines, specific quality thresholds were set. High-quality and “recommended” guidelines were those with scores ≥70% for all domains; moderate quality and “recommended with modifications” guidelines were those with scores ≥70% in three to five domains; low-quality and not recommended guidelines were those with scores ≥70% in none of the domains or up to two domains. 3. Results Results of the evaluations of the 11 clinical practice guidelines can be found in . Three clinical practice guidelines were found to be of moderate quality [ , , ]. High-quality clinical guidelines for the nutritional management of patients with CKD were not found according to the parameters of the AGREE II tool. The lowest score, i.e., one point per reviewer, is equal to 14.3% in terms of percentage in the AGREE tool II and reflects either the poor description of the relevant information or its total absence from the guideline. 3.1. Scope and Purpose Domain The majority of the clinical practice guidelines received high ratings in the domain of “scope and purpose”, while six of them received a score ≥70% [ , , , , , ]. Four guidelines received low scores [ , , , ] and the EBPG guideline received the lowest [ ]. 3.2. Stakeholder Involvement Domain In this domain, none of the included guidelines were highly rated by the four reviewers. Five studies had rates of 40–70%, which translates into a moderate quality [ , , , , ], whereas in the remaining six studies had rate scores <40%, leading to low-quality characterization [ , , , , , ]. Item 2b, “target population’s views and preferences”, was sufficiently stated in only two guidelines (DAA and SIN-ANDIN-ANED) [ , ]. Moreover, item 2a, which refers to the expertise and the roles of members taking part in the guideline development group, was only reported in the KDOQI guidelines [ ]. 3.3. Rigor of Development Τhe results for the domain “rigor of development” varied. This domain evaluates all stages of the methodological development of each guideline review as well as information on the update process. The highest score can be observed in the KDOQI guidelines [ ], whereas in the other guidelines many items of this domain were not included [ , , , , , , , ] or were not satisfactorily described [ , ]. 3.4. Clarity of Presentation Regarding the clarity of

taking part in the guideline development group, was only reported in the KDOQI guidelines [ ]. 3.3. Rigor of Development Τhe results for the domain “rigor of development” varied. This domain evaluates all stages of the methodological development of each guideline review as well as information on the update process. The highest score can be observed in the KDOQI guidelines [ ], whereas in the other guidelines many items of this domain were not included [ , , , , , , , ] or were not satisfactorily described [ , ]. 3.4. Clarity of Presentation Regarding the clarity of presentation, the results were satisfactory. Clinical practice guidelines developed by DGEM received the highest scores (100) [ ]. High scores were also reported in seven clinical practice guidelines which scored >70% [ , , , , , , ] and three guidelines were determined to be of moderate quality [ , , ]. None of the guidelines received a low score for this domain. 3.5. Applicability As per the domain of “Applicability”, none of the included clinical practice guidelines received a total score ≥70%. Moreover ASPEN, SIN-ANDID-ANED and the Renal Association received scores of zero as they failed to mention this aspect in their manuscripts [ , , ]. 3.6. Editorial Independence In this domain, the reviewers appraised the included clinical practice guidelines according to the information provided for the funding and the authors’ conflicts of interest during the guideline development. In eight guidelines, exclusive funding statements were found [ , , , , , , , ], but information on whether this funding influenced the content of guidelines was not always reported (i.e., DGEM, EDTNA-ERCA, and SIN-ANDID-ANED guidelines [ , , ]). In the ASPEN and DAA guidelines, no funding existed [ , ]. Moreover, statements of competing interest were not found in the ASPEN and GARIN guidelines [ , ]. The average quality score of each domain between recommended with modifications and not recommended guidelines can be seen in and a summary of the AGREE II tool results of each domain can be found in . 4. Discussion The aim of the present study was to assess the quality of development of 11 nutritional guidelines for patients with CKD using the AGREE II tool [ ]. According to our results, scores between the domains of each guideline differed significantly. Clinical guidelines developed by the KDOQI received the highest rating (≥70% in four domains) [ ], followed by ESPEN (EN) and DAA guidelines (≥70% in three domains) [ , ] and were recommended with modifications by the reviewers. Moreover, clinical guidelines by ASPEN, DGEM, EBPG, EDTNA–ERCA, ESPEN (PN), GARIN, SIN–ANDID–ANED, and the Renal Association [ , , , , , , , ] were characterized by a low overall quality and thus were not recommended based on the AGREE II tool [ ]. Based on the AGREE II reported items, there are several fields in the quality of guidelines that could be improved. In general, sufficient evidence for the purpose and scope (Domain 1) can be found in the guidelines studied. Regarding this domain, EPBG [ ] and the Renal Association [ ] failed to clearly describe the population covered by the guidelines. Clarifying purpose and scope can prohibit the use of guidelines for a nonappropriate group of patients. As for the stakeholder involvement (Domain 2), more information about expertise, geographical location as well as the role of each member in guideline development could improve the significance of EDTNA-ERCA, GARIN, and the Renal Association guidelines [ , , ], as an emphasis on multidisciplinary approaches could have a positive impact on the quality of the guidelines. Population experiences and expectations were not adequately described in the included guidelines and this should be considered for the future updated versions. Moreover, target users’ information is missing in the EBPG [ ] guideline, which should be clearly defined so as the clinician can recognize whether the guideline is appropriate for his/her use. As per rigor of development (Domain 3), the intense heterogeneity that was found between the scores ( ) proves the existence of significant gaps regarding the guidelines’ methodological development. Only in the KDOQI [ ] guideline description and methods of evidence selection were described. This is the domain in which several modifications are needed (i.e., better description of research methodology, report of included/excluded criteria, strengths and potential limitations of guideline development, link between scientific evidence and recommendations, etc.) in order to improve the quality of the existing clinical practice guidelines. In most of the guidelines examined, recommendations were clearly presented (Domain 4), facilitating the easy accessibility and application by the clinician, something that is important especially in acute settings. Tables, summarizing boxes, bold font, and/or numbers were used in all analyzed nutritional guidelines and/or key recommendations. Moreover, only in the

evidence selection were described. This is the domain in which several modifications are needed (i.e., better description of research methodology, report of included/excluded criteria, strengths and potential limitations of guideline development, link between scientific evidence and recommendations, etc.) in order to improve the quality of the existing clinical practice guidelines. In most of the guidelines examined, recommendations were clearly presented (Domain 4), facilitating the easy accessibility and application by the clinician, something that is important especially in acute settings. Tables, summarizing boxes, bold font, and/or numbers were used in all analyzed nutritional guidelines and/or key recommendations. Moreover, only in the SIN-ANDID-ANED guideline [ ], the item of different options for management in patients with CKD was not satisfactorily described, a parameter that indicates that a different approach according to stage and the severity of CKD is needed, as claimed by the majority of included guidelines. An important parameter that should be highlighted is that although the AGREE II tool includes the item regarding different options for management, consideration of the patient’s condition in the very beginning of their treatment is missing. None of the 11 guidelines examined included satisfactory statements for the first approach according to the condition of the patient. For example, novel, ketogenic diets, prescribed by trained physicians, could prove helpful for obese patients with mild CKD [ , ], but in recently published guidelines, special recommendations for this group of patients were not stated. As per applicability, an important domain of the AGREE II instrument (Domain 5), all nutritional guidelines failed to adequately report facilitators and barriers and/or provide tools, advice, and potential resources that can affect implementation in clinical practice; consequently, in all guidelines, the total obtained score for this domain was <70%. The best described item of this domain was that of monitoring, which was only not applicable for ASPEN, SIN-ANDID-ANED, and the Renal Association clinical practice guidelines [ , , ]. Finally, the evidence of funding and/or conflicts of interest were not informative in all cases. Only in the DAA [ ] clinical practice guideline was editorial independence (Domain 6) entirely described. The fact that funding body information and/or competing interest statements are not clearly and adequately described can be associated with several biases regarding the content of recommendations. As the AGREE II tool can sufficiently identify the problematic areas in the clinical practice guidelines, it is highly recommended that this tool should be used by guidelines developers as a checklist with a view to keeping structure and adequacy in guideline development methodology and to ensuring the high quality of the guidelines produced. Our study has several strengths. First, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that compares and evaluates the quality of the clinical practice guidelines in nutritional management of patients with CKD. Moreover, the assessment and rating of the eligible guidelines was performed independently by a multidisciplinary group of four reviewers, including medical doctors and dieticians. Furthermore, it is the first time that the AGREE II tool has been used for the quality evaluation of the nutritional practice guidelines for CKD. One of the limitations of our study is that we included guidelines in English, Spanish, and German and we may have excluded other published guidelines in different languages. Moreover, the fact that nine out of 11 guidelines included in our study came from European regions could mean that the results of our study might be difficult to be applied to patients in other regions. In addition, the appraisal tool does not provide standard cut offs for the evaluation of scores and this could affect the interpretation of our results. Furthermore, it should be clarified that in this study, only the critical appraisal of the quality development of the guidelines was performed without any assessment of the quality of the guidelines’ content. 5. Conclusions The quality of the development of the majority of the nutritional clinical practice guidelines on management of CKD patients it is not satisfactory. The guidelines that were the best in terms of quality according to the AGREE II tool were the KDOQI, DAA, and ESPEN (EN), ensuring a better quality of information, even if they all require modifications in future update processes [ , , ]. Additionally, as several gaps in methodology development were identified in most of the guidelines, the following updates should incorporate these changes in order to ameliorate their quality. Editorial independence should be described in detail in order to eliminate bias. AGREE II can be a useful tool in the evaluation of quality of clinical practice guidelines.

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Pancreatic involvement in cystic fibrosis (CF) is well known since the earliest descriptions noted by Dr. Dorothy Andersen in the 1930s [ ]. People with CF (pwCF) have reduced production of pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate due to CF transmembrane regulator (CFTR) protein dysfunction [ ]. Approximately 85%−90% of pwCF of all ages have severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI), and the remaining CF population have preserved pancreatic function, which is referred to as exocrine pancreatic sufficiency (EPS) [ , , , , , , , ]. Unlike the pulmonary manifestations, the pancreatic phenotype correlates well with the severity of the genotype [ ]. Over 95% of pwCF with severe mutations (class I, II, or III) in both alleles have EPI, and the manifestations of EPI develop when the postprandial enzyme output is < 5%−10% of normal [ , , , , , ]. In pwCF, pancreatic damage starts in utero, and approximately 60% of all infants with CF have EPI at birth [ , ]. The remaining 20%−25% infants may have loss of exocrine pancreatic function due to ongoing pancreatic inflammation and/or obstruction after birth or in the first few years of life, accounting for a total of 85% of pwCF having EPI [ , ]. In contrast, most people with two mild (class IV and V) mutations or one mild plus one severe mutation usually have EPS at birth [ , , , ]. However, it should be noted that the presence of one mild mutation does not exclude EPI, necessitating the need for objective evaluation of exocrine pancreatic function [ ]. Identification of EPI as soon as possible after the diagnosis of CF is important to minimize steatorrhea and subsequent malnutrition. Currently, fecal elastase‐1 (FE‐1) is the most widely used for evaluating exocrine pancreatic status. The fundamental aspects of different types of exocrine pancreatic function tests including FE‐1, their advantages, disadvantages, and technical considerations, are detailed in the Supporting Information Document. Before the advent of FE‐1, most pwCF were diagnosed with EPI on clinical grounds (presence of gastrointestinal symptoms, growth failure, and fat‐soluble vitamin deficiencies), and pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) was prescribed mostly based on these clinical manifestations [ , ]. Some investigators classify infants with EPI if two EPI‐causing CFTR mutations are identified [ , ]. However, this method is prone to error and may overestimate EPI [ ]. Objective evaluation of pancreatic status is essential as pwCF can be erroneously classified as EPS or EPI based on clinical manifestations or genetic mutations alone. For example, in a study by Baker and colleagues enrolling 1215 participants, 1131 (93.1%) were prescribed PERT. FE‐1 analysis identified 1074 (89%) people with EPI (defined as FE‐1 value < 200 μg/g of stool), demonstrating the differences between subjective perception and objective confirmation of EPI [ ]. Once considered permanent, with the advent of CFTR‐directed therapies (modulators), improvements in exocrine pancreatic function and conversion from EPI to EPS have been reported in a smaller percentage of pwCF based on FE‐1 measurements [ ]. However, there are no current guidelines regarding monitoring of exocrine pancreatic status, particularly post‐initiation of CFTR‐directed therapies. In this review, we aimed to evaluate studies that investigated FE‐1 in pwCF to identify the gaps in our understanding and what is known can be applied in current clinical practice. 2 Methodology We performed a scoping review due to heterogeneity of the studies and the risk of bias [ , ]. The initial search period was from 1‐1‐2003 to 7‐31‐2025. Studies on FE‐1 included a wide range of patient population (neonates/infants, children, and adults), different diagnostic methods for EPI and EPS, and variable FE‐1 cut off values for defining EPI [ , ]. Due to this wide variation in populations, interventions, and outcomes, a formal quality assessment such as a systematic review or meta‐analysis was not feasible. For this scoping review, we followed the framework for scoping reviews as outlined by the JBI guidance for scoping reviews, which was detailed by Peters et al., and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) statement [ , ]. Institutional review board approval was not required as this review did not involve direct human research. The details of the search strategy, study selection, and data extraction were detailed the Supporting Information Document. A PRISMA flow diagram was auto‐generated in Covidence and modified to include the pertinent details (Figure ), and data were presented in descriptive format. For this review, we did not use artificial intelligence generated content tools such as ChatGPT and others based on large language models. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta‐Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA‐ScR) checklist was also included in the Supporting Information Document. We combined the studies to synthesize information on four important questions, which are detailed below in the results section.

We combined the studies to synthesize information on four important questions, which are detailed below in the results section. 3 Results 3.1 Utilization of FE‐1 in CF (When to Screen for EPI and How Often to Screen) Determination of EPI at the time of CF diagnosis (either by newborn screening or diagnosis at a later age) to elucidate the pancreatic phenotype is mandatory to determine if the patient needs PERT and CF‐specific vitamins immediately to prevent malnutrition‐related consequences [ , , , , ]. Experts and most CF guidelines recommend obtaining FE‐1 after 2 weeks of age in infants with CF diagnosed by prenatal/newborn screening [ , , , , , ]. The CF Foundation (CFF) 2009 infant guidelines recommended estimation of exocrine pancreatic function for all infants with CF and PERT to be initiated with an FE‐1 < 200 µg/g or coefficient of fat absorption (CFA) < 85% for infants less than 6 months of age, or in infants with two CF mutations associated with EPI (while waiting for the stool‐based testing) [ ]. Common symptoms of EPI include steatorrhea and weight loss/poor weight gain despite increased appetite, but these symptoms are neither sensitive in early stages nor specific for EPI [ ]. Also, the infant guidelines recommended not initiating PERT in infants less than 2 years of life with one or two CFTR mutations associated with EPS unless an objective test confirms the EPI status [ ]. In a study by Barben et al, the addition of FE‐1 to the newborn screening protocol reduced the time to the diagnosis of CF in a population who had CF‐screen positive but had an inconclusive CF diagnosis [ ]. Before the advent of FE‐1, PERT was usually initiated based on subjective gastrointestinal symptoms, and this practice is not currently recommended [ ]. Further, a short‐term therapeutic trial of PERT to see if the gastrointestinal symptoms improve or not is also not reliable to establish a diagnosis of EPI as these symptoms are neither sensitive nor specific for EPI [ ]. For infants with CF and EPS at diagnosis, annual evaluation of FE‐1 is recommended to monitor pancreatic exocrine status. Earlier reevaluation should be done if there are concerns for growth failure or declining nutritional status, or if pwCF have two CFTR mutations previously reported to be strongly associated with EPI (mutations in the CFTR gene class I, II, or III) [ , , , , , ]. On the other hand, in people with EPS with mutations known to offer residual CFTR function (classes IV and V mutations in the CFTR gene), FE‐1 can be checked annually during infancy and less frequently during childhood [ , , , , ]. Infants with CF may exhibit variability in FE‐1 during the first year. EPI is less prevalent in infancy than later in life, suggesting plasticity of pancreatic function early in life. Approximately 60% of infants diagnosed with CF via newborn screening have EPI at birth [ ]. Many infants initially found to have EPS at birth may have ongoing pancreatic obstruction and inflammation leading to EPI in the first few years of life; thus, 85%‐90% of pwCF have EPI [ , , , , , , , , , , ]. Even infants with FE‐1 values consistent with EPI may have fluctuating levels during the first year of life, which provides a rationale for why pancreatic function may improve in infants given CFTR modulators. In a longitudinal study, 61 infants in the pre‐modulator era had an initial stool sample obtained at age < 3.5 months, samples were obtained monthly, and a final stool sample was obtained at age > 9 months [ ]. Of the 48 infants with initial FE‐1 < 200 μg/g, 27% (13/48) had at least one FE‐1 > 200 μg/g, but had a final FE‐1 < 200 μg/g; however, 8% (4/48) of these infants ended the year with a value > 200 μg/g [ ]. Thirteen infants had an initial FE‐1 > 200 μg/g. Of these, 85% (11/13) still had a value > 200 μg/g at the end of infancy [ ]. This is especially true in the era of CFTR modulators, which may modify pancreatic function as discussed below. FE‐1 should ideally be re‐measured in infants during the first year of life to ensure that those with EPI receive PERT and those who may recover function do not continue to receive PERT unnecessarily [ , ]. Defining pancreatic functional status with FE‐1 also has implications for clinical follow‐up beyond infancy. A small proportion of people with EPS with residual CFTR protein function may develop recurrent pancreatitis with damage to pancreatic parenchyma, eventually progressing to EPI at a later age [ , , , ]. However, if a patient with EPS has low FE‐1 in the EPI range after an episode of acute pancreatitis, FE‐1 should be reevaluated 6 months later, as these patients may have transient EPI after acute pancreatitis [ , ]. In a large multinational cohort, pancreatitis was noted mainly during adolescence and young adulthood, with an approximate prevalence of 61 cases in 3306 pwCF (1.84%) [ ]. Pancreatitis is much more common among pwCF and EPS (~10%) vs pwCF with EPI (0.5%) [ ]. Similar observations were made by other investigators as well [ , , , , ]. Pancreatitis occurred in 14% (20 out of 139) of pwCF with EPS in a study done in Israel [ ]. Four out of these 20 pwCF (20%) who had EPS later developed EPI, emphasizing that pwCF with EPS are at increased risk of recurrent pancreatitis and at risk of subsequent development of EPI [ ]. This emphasizes the importance of repeated monitoring of FE‐1 in pwCF with residual function mutations [ ]. Recent data suggest improvement in EPI in some young children after the introduction of highly effective modulators. Even though evidence‐based guidelines are lacking, many experts recommend testing the FE‐1 6 months after the introduction of highly effective modulators, and this is further detailed later in this review [ ]. They enrolled 28 pwCF aged 4−20 years. The sensitivity of FE‐1 with a cut‐off point of 200 µg/g was 89.3% for all pwCF. The sensitivity was 100% for pwCF in the moderate to severe EPI categories, but was only 25% for people in the mild category; the specificity of FE‐1 was 96.4%. Linear regression analysis showed a statistically significant correlation between FE‐1 and duodenal volume, bicarbonate, amylase, lipase, and trypsin secretion (in all categories of EPI severity, p < 0.001). In pwCF and EPI, FE‐1 is highly sensitive and specific, but it is less accurate in pwCF with EPS. Soldan included 16 pwCF with 23 healthy controls and used secretin‐pancreozymin‐based pancreatic stimulation test and FFE as standard tests for EPI and compared FE‐1 [ ]. All pwCF had moderate to severe EPI based on pancreatic stimulation testing. They noted FE‐1 < 200 µg/g demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 96% specificity [ ]. Comparing 72‐h FFE, FE‐1 demonstrated a sensitivity of 98.7% in pwCF with EPI status but only 50% sensitivity in pwCF with EPS [ ]. Weintraub studied pwCF and EPS based on CFA and noted similar results [ ]. Engjom et al used FE‐1 as the reference test and evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a short‐timed endoscopic secretin test [ ]. They recruited 31 pwCF (both EPS and EPI participants) and 25 healthy controls. People with FE‐1 < 100 μg/g were considered to have EPI. In many places of the world, secretin is no longer easily available, making the evaluation of bicarbonate secretion challenging. Fecal chymotrypsin has been available as a measure of pancreatic function since the 1980s [ ]. Fecal chymotrypsin tests measure the total amount of chymotrypsin in a stool sample, and PERT must be stopped prior to testing, unlike measurement of FE‐1 [ ]. Later, fecal lipase was also investigated for EPI evaluation. FE‐1 is more specific and sensitive compared to both fecal chymotrypsin and lipase when comparing all these tests to direct pancreatic stimulation [ , , , ]. Walkowiak et al compared FE‐1 and fecal lipase with 72‐h FFE and secretin‐cholecystokinin tests (used as reference tests in this study) [ ]. The sensitivity and specificity of fecal lipase were compared to FE‐1 in 90 pwCF and in 95 healthy controls. With the cut‐off levels providing the same specificity for both FE‐1 and fecal lipase (at 95.8%), the sensitivity of the FE‐1 test was higher (91.1%) when compared to the fecal lipase test (76.7%), p < 0.0036. Sample‐to‐sample and day‐to‐day variations were significantly lower for FE‐1 than for fecal lipase measurements, p < 0.0001. A study from Brazil explored the alternative testing strategies when FE‐1 is not available in resource‐limited settings for diagnosing EPI in infants. FE‐1 was utilized as the reference test and compared with 72‐h FFE, steatocrit, and low weight gain (<50th percentile of daily weight gain) as alternatives for FE‐1 [ ]. EPI was defined when FE‐1 < 200 μg/gm; 39 infants with CF were included. There was a high specificity (100%) and PPV (100%) between FE‐1 and FFE, but low sensitivity (58%) and NPV (46.7%) were noted. In combination, low weight gain and abnormal steatocrit showed 91% sensitivity and 83% specificity for EPI diagnosis. Non‐fecal tests are rapidly gaining popularity due to the difficulties surrounding stool collection from patients. Investigators have explored the 13C‐mixed triglyceride (13C‐MTG) breath test and imaging modalities such as the secretin‐based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [ , , ]. The 13C‐MTG is a noninvasive test that utilizes non‐radioisotopic (13C‐tagged MTG given in a liquid meal) and measures how well pancreatic lipase can digest lipids. In the presence of lipase, the 13C‐MTG is digested into free fatty acids and monoglycerides, which are absorbed in the gut and reach the liver. In the liver, they are oxidized to 13C‐labeled carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), which is measured in breath samples using spectrometry. This method is popular in Europe but is not available in the USA [ , ]. Kent et al compared the 13C‐MTG breath test and FE‐1 (both monoclonal and polyclonal assays) with 72‐h FFE in infants with CF [ ]. The sensitivity rates were high for both the 13C‐MTG breath test and the FE‐1 (82%−100%) for pwCF with EPI. Low‐sensitivity rates were noted for CF with EPS for both these tests. Sensitivity of the 13C‐MTG breath test was 31%–38% when compared with the monoclonal FE‐1 test (46%–54%) and the polyclonal FE‐1 test (45%). PwCF and EPS produce approximately 40% less pancreatic fluid compared to people without CF, and this property has been utilized in secretin‐stimulated MRI (s‐MRI) [ , ]. In a study from Poland involving a small number of pwCF with EPS (defined as FE‐1 > 200 µg/g) and healthy controls, the width of the pancreatic duct in secretin‐enhanced magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) was smaller and significantly different in pwCF compared to the non‐CF controls [ ]. However, the same group of investigators did not find any meaningful difference in width size between CF‐EPI, defined as FE‐1 < 100 µg/g, and CF‐EPS [ ]. In another study, Engjom et al compared FE‐1 (reference test in this study) versus s‐MRI [ ]. The diagnostic accuracy of s‐MRI in estimating exocrine pancreatic function was compared in pwCF ( N = 21) and healthy controls ( N = 42). EPI was defined as FE‐1 < 200 μg/g or duodenal bicarbonate concentration < 80 mmol/L. EPI was noted in 11/21 pwCF. Participants with EPI had lower s‐MRI volume output compared with all other groups ( p < 0.05). The s‐MRI yielded a diagnostic accuracy of 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.90–1) for defining EPI in CF. Further, the discrepancy in findings regarding the utility and discriminating performance of s‐MRI between the three groups (CF‐EPI, CF‐EPS, and healthy controls) was very dramatically different and concerning. Participants with EPI had lower s‐MRI volume output compared with all other groups ( p < 0.05). The s‐MRI yielded a diagnostic accuracy of 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.90–1) for defining EPI in CF. Further, the discrepancy in findings regarding the utility and discriminating performance of s‐MRI between the three groups (CF‐EPI, CF‐EPS, and healthy controls) was very dramatically different and concerning. The high cost involved in this method and the need for anesthesia in younger and uncooperative patients limit its utility for screening EPI in CF. As noted above, secretin is no longer easily available, adding challenges in the administration of this test. In summary, among all the tests (both direct and indirect tests for EPI in CF), FE‐1 remains a simple and reliable screening test for evaluation of exocrine pancreatic function. The diagnostic utility of FE‐1 versus other EPI‐1 tests is summarized in Tables and . 3.3 Definition of Ideal Cut‐Off for FE‐1 in Evaluating EPI in CF Most CF studies included the cut‐off of <200 µg/g for EPI as recommended by the first manufacturer to bring this test to the market (ScheBo Biotech, Giessen, Germany) [ , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Walkowiak et al noted the best cut‐off to differentiate CF with EPI and normal pancreatic function in healthy controls as 184 μg/g or a range between 160 and 200 μg/g [ ]. With a cut‐off of 132 µg/g of stool, the sensitivity and specificity of FE‐1 were noted as 96% and 100%, respectively, in children with CF [ ]. Values between 100 and 199 are considered as mild to moderate EPI, and < 100 µg/g as severe EPI [ , , ]. Generally, in most pwCF with EPI, the average FE‐1 is lower < 50 µg/g, and one study demonstrated that the median (IQR) value of FE‐1 was 10 µg/g (2.5−33) of stool [ ]. Based on the 2023 CFF Patient Registry, about 72% of infants with CF born in 2023 had FE‐1 estimation, which is an increase from <60% reported for infants born in 2013 [ ]. Most of the individuals (850/872) with a known FE‐1 value of <200 µg/g were prescribed PERT; however, 2.5% (22/872) did not receive PERT [ ]. Also, 29% (75/259) of the population who had FE‐1 ≥ 200 µg/g of stool were prescribed PERT based on clinical grounds [ ]. The Baby Observational and NUtrition Study (BONUS) also noted similar trends to the 2023 CFF Patient Registry [ ]. The CFF infant clinical care guidelines recommended PERT be initiated for all infants with two CFTR variants associated with EPI, an FE‐1 value < 200 μg/g of stool, and/or signs and symptoms of malabsorption (while awaiting confirmatory FE‐1 results) [ ]. The 2008 CFF consensus report stated that FE‐1 values between 100 and 200 μg/g are considered indicative of mild to moderate EPI, although not necessarily of sufficient severity to warrant the need for routine PERT supplementation if the patient does not have manifestations of fat malabsorption [ ]. The 2024 ESPGHAN‐ESPEN‐ECF states that FE‐1 values ≤ 100 μg/g stool are diagnostic of EPI and labels values between 100 and 200 μg/g as “borderline.” A recent systematic review and meta‐analysis included seven CF studies that compared FE‐1 with CFA. This study demonstrated a high sensitivity of 0.98 (IQR of 0.77‐0.99) for FE‐1 in CF when a cut‐off of <200 µg/g is used [ , , , , , , , ]. With a lower cut‐off of <100 µg/g, the sensitivity decreased to 0.85 (IQR of 0.54−0.97), but the specificity of FE‐1 did not change significantly between the two cut‐offs [ ]. The specificity was 0.62 when the FE‐1 cut‐off was <200 µg/g and was 0.65 when the cut‐off was <100 µg/g [ ]. There is considerable debate on the appropriate cut point for treatment, although some experts recommend treatment only for FE‐1 values < 100 µg/g with close follow‐up for pwCF with FE‐1 between 100 and 200 µg/g [ ]. As the consequences of untreated EPI are severe, a higher sensitivity of FE‐1 (using FE‐1 < 200 µg/g as a screening test for EPI) is preferable over specificity. Individual day‐to‐day variations in FE‐1 are generally low [ , ]. In 10 pwCF‐EPI, repeated measures of FE‐1 using a monoclonal test kit gave an intra‐assay variation of 7.0% and inter‐assay variation of 7.2% [ ]. Studies have noted a mean coefficient of variation (CV) for FE‐1 anywhere between <10% and 26% for pwCF with EPI [ , , , ]. Hamwi et al noted

between 100 and 200 µg/g [ ]. As the consequences of untreated EPI are severe, a higher sensitivity of FE‐1 (using FE‐1 < 200 µg/g as a screening test for EPI) is preferable over specificity. Individual day‐to‐day variations in FE‐1 are generally low [ , ]. In 10 pwCF‐EPI, repeated measures of FE‐1 using a monoclonal test kit gave an intra‐assay variation of 7.0% and inter‐assay variation of 7.2% [ ]. Studies have noted a mean coefficient of variation (CV) for FE‐1 anywhere between <10% and 26% for pwCF with EPI [ , , , ]. Hamwi et al noted a mean CV of 22% in eight participants within one stool passage and further demonstrated a mean CV of 26% from day‐to‐day variation in 40 participants [ ]. Here, the authors recommended a routine analysis of more than one stool sample to be collected on different days for FE‐1 and to use a range of ±25% of the recommended cut‐off of 200 µg/g for the diagnosis of EPI [ ]. However, if FE‐1 is between 100 and 200 µg/g, clinicians should strongly consider EPI (specifically considering the above‐mentioned CV of FE‐1). At the same time, the presence of other possible causes of low FE‐1 should also be considered and evaluated. Other than EPI, low FE‐1 can occur if stools are watery (dilution effect), or in people with diminished signaling of the pancreas due to enteropathy (severe malnutrition, post‐infectious state, celiac disease, or Crohn's disease) or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (“secondary EPI”) [ ]. 3.4 Utilizing FE‐1 in pwCF Treated With CFTR‐Directed Therapies Ivacaftor—CFTR modulating drugs have had a dramatic effect on pulmonary health and a variable effect on pancreatic health as measured by FE‐1. Ivacaftor improved exocrine pancreatic function (as indicated by FE‐1 > 200 µg/g) in approximately 26%−67% of children 1−5 years of age in various registration studies [ , , , ]. Others have reported an increase in FE‐1 in some pwCF taking ivacaftor after it was available for clinical use [ , , , , , , , ]. However, in a study involving pwCF between 5 and 61 years, Stallings et al did not show any significant improvement of FE‐1 after ivacaftor [ ]. In another scoping review that evaluated pancreatic function after exposure to CFTR modulators (mostly ivacaftor), individual‐level data were reported in 34 subjects. Those who converted to EPS‐CF were more likely to have a detectable FE‐1 at baseline (75% vs. 0%, p < 0.001) and were younger (median 5.9 vs. 8.4 years, p = 0.003), but there was no difference in treatment duration [ ]. Dual modulators—Improvement in FE‐1 has also been noted with less efficacious dual modulators directed at pwCF homozygous for the F508del‐CFTR mutation, such as the combination of lumacaftor and ivacaftor, and this improvement is also noted to be better in young children [ , , ]. Three of 48 children with EPI attained EPS at the end of 24 weeks of treatment [ ]. However, during the 2‐week washout period, the EPS status was lost in some patients, which emphasizes the rapidly reversible nature of the exocrine pancreatic improvement with these therapies [ ]. Similarly, in the study involving 49 children with CF by Imrei et al, one child (above 12 years of age) had FE‐1 > 200 μg/g at baseline, and after 24 months of lumacaftor and ivacaftor, three more children had FE‐1 > 200 μg/g [ ]. Among these three children, two were between 2 and 5 years of age, and one child was between 6 and 11 years of age [ ]. Crowley et al noted restoration of pancreatic function with lumacaftor and ivacaftor in a toddler whose baseline FE‐1 was 33 μg/g at age 8 months and <15 μg/g at 22 months. She commenced on lumacaftor and ivacaftor at age 24 months. A repeat FE‐1 at 3 years 4 months was 489 μg/g. In contrast, in children between 2 and 6 years from the USA and Canada who started on lumacaftor and ivacaftor, no significant increase in FE‐1 was reported [ ]. Among 19 children between ages 2−5 years, the baseline mean ± SE FE‐1 was 15 ± 0 μg/g, and at the end of 24 weeks, the mean ± SE FE‐1 in 19 participants was 29 ± 9.5 ( p value −0.07) [ ]. Improvement in FE‐1 has been noted in other studies with lumacaftor and ivacaftor. Generally, the younger the patient is, the higher the likelihood of improved pancreatic function [ , , , ]. Similarly, improvement in EPI has been noted in a small number of pwCF after tezacaftor and ivacaftor. In the study by Rowe et al, three groups were compared: tezacaftor and ivacaftor, ivacaftor, and placebo [ ]. Among pwCF with FE‐1 values < 200 μg/g at study baseline, 6

24 weeks, the mean ± SE FE‐1 in 19 participants was 29 ± 9.5 ( p value −0.07) [ ]. Improvement in FE‐1 has been noted in other studies with lumacaftor and ivacaftor. Generally, the younger the patient is, the higher the likelihood of improved pancreatic function [ , , , ]. Similarly, improvement in EPI has been noted in a small number of pwCF after tezacaftor and ivacaftor. In the study by Rowe et al, three groups were compared: tezacaftor and ivacaftor, ivacaftor, and placebo [ ]. Among pwCF with FE‐1 values < 200 μg/g at study baseline, 6 (27%) in the tezacaftor and ivacaftor group, 4 (18%) in the ivacaftor group, and 1 (5%) in the placebo group had maximum FE‐1 values ≥ 200 μg/g at week 4 and week 8 [ ]. Triple modulators—With the advent of the highly efficacious modulator, elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), currently ~92% of pwCF in the U.S. are either receiving modulators or are eligible for modulators [ ]. In the PROMISE‐GI study involving 99 pwCF aged > 12 years, the overall adjusted increase in FE‐1 was only 7.08 μg/g (3.58, 10.58) with 6 months of ETI therapy, and was not clinically significant [ ]. Similarly, in another multicenter study in pwCF > 18 years of age, no significant change in FE‐1 was noted after 6 months of ETI therapy [ ]. An increase in FE‐1 was noted with increasing duration of ETI therapy in children with CF above 2–5 years of age. At baseline, 2/75 (2.7%) had EPS, which increased to 6/75 (8%) at week 24, and 13/70 (18.6%) at week 48 [ ]. Various pediatric studies with smaller samples noted improvement in FE‐1 in pwCF [ , , , , ]. In multiple case reports, intrauterine management of CF with ETI has resulted in normal pancreatic function of babies at birth [ , , , , , , , ]. However, in others who received ETI in utero, pancreatic insufficiency did not improve [ ]. A new triple combination CFTR modulator is now available (Vanzacaftor + Tezacaftor + Deutivacaftor), and we await data on its effect on FE‐1. In the recent guidance focused on pwCF post‐ETI published by CF nutrition experts, FE‐1 retesting was recommended 6 months after ETI initiation and annually thereafter, as some (mostly younger children) may recover sufficient exocrine pancreatic function over time [ ]. As noted earlier, the chances of improvement in FE‐1 increase with the duration of modulator therapies, pragmatically, FE‐1 testing can be recommended between 6 and 12 months of modulator therapy. FE‐1 levels > 200 μg/g do not always exclude EPI (mild or moderate), and interpretation of EPI should be made within the broader clinical context [ ]. By expert consensus, it was recommended that if the FE‐1 is consistently between 200 and 500 μg/g, PERT can be gradually tapered off (not abruptly stopped) [ ]. They further recommended close monitoring of growth, gastrointestinal symptoms, and nutrient absorption if the PERT dosage is reduced [ ]. The gradual stepwise de‐escalation of PERT and not abrupt cessation after attaining EPS was further elaborated in a recent review by Ramsey and Ooi [ ]. 4 Conclusion and Future Directions Of the available tests, FE‐1 is the best screening test for estimating pancreatic exocrine function in CF at the present time. All pwCF should have pancreatic status evaluated at diagnosis. FE‐1 should be evaluated if there is a change in clinical status (e.g., decreased weight gain in those with EPS or pancreatitis in pwCF with EPI). In pwCF, FE‐1 < 200 µg/g is highly sensitive, and FE‐1 < 100 µg/g of stool is highly specific for EPI. CFTR modulators, especially ivacaftor and ETI, have been associated with improvements in pancreatic functional status, mostly in infants and younger children. A reevaluation of FE‐1 at least 6 months after initiation of CFTR‐directed highly effective modulators is recommended. Future prospective trials investigating the evolution of exocrine pancreatic function in the current era of modulators are urgently needed.
